articles.title: Mexican special forces arrest drug kingpin 'Chapo Isidro'
articles.summary: The alleged leader of the Beltran Leyva gang and one of the FBI's most wanted fugitives, known as 'Chapo Isidro,' was captured by the Mexican military following a raid and a shootout in the coastal…

image.caption: Mexico's military said they have detained 'Chapo Isidro' alongside his second-in-command and a financial operatorImage: Mexican Secretariat of National Defense/AFP

blocks.text: A gun battle between Mexican soldiers and alleged gang members in the city of Guasave, in the state of Sinaloa, ended with special forces detaining senior members of the Beltran Leyva drug trafficking network, Mexican officials said on Saturday.
The gang is aligned with one of the factions of the powerful Sinaloa cartel.
Authorities said the overnight raid resulted in capture of the suspected drug kingpin Fausto Isidro Meza F., better known as "Chapo Isidro," who is believed to be the leader of Beltran Leyva.
FBI offering millions for 'Chapo Isidro'

The 44-year-old Mexican national is one of the FBI's ten most wanted fugitives. The US law enforcement agency claims his group is responsible for smuggling "large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl, and marijuana into the United States," and has offered a $5 million (€4.56 million) reward for information leading to his arrest.
He is also wanted in Mexico on charges including organized crime.
On Saturday, Mexican authorities said the raid was conducted due to "intelligence coordination" between Mexico's military and US agencies.
The three detainees were transported to Mexico City "to be placed at the disposal of the competent prosecutorial authorities," the military said.
It was not immediately clear if "Chapo Isidro" will be extradited to the US.
Roads blocked in Sinaloa
The troops used "stealth and surprise" to reach the area, establishing a perimeter around the drug dealer's location and then moving in from multiple directions, according Mexico's US embassy.

Unverified videos from Guasave, however, showed military helicopters firing at ground targets and sports fans scrambling for safety during a baseball game. Some of the violence in the western Mexican city seems to have taken place after Chapo Isidro was arrested, with drug cartels attempting to retaliate against the authorities and civilians for the move.

blocks.caption: The military said security forces were deployed to restore traffic on roads and highways in Mexico's SinaloaImage: Yohari Leon/REUTERS

blocks.text: Mexico's defense ministry confirmed cartel members set up roadblocks in the area, but added that security forces were assisting local authorities in restoring order.

The Guasave raid is only the latest in a string of high-profile moves against senior leaders of Mexico's illegal drug trade. Less than two weeks ago, Mexican navy announced the arrest of Rafael A., suspected of leading a cartel cell active in the states of Jalisco and Michoacan.
President ​Claudia Sheinbaum is facing pressure from Donald Trump, who has threatened to take military action against cartels on Mexican territory.

Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspects, victims and those who are associated with a criminal case, and urges the media to refrain from publishing their full identities in most cases.

articles.title: Russia-bound ship attacked in Gulf of Finland
articles.summary: Finnish defence forces say that Ukraine was likely behind the drone attack on the vessel.

blocks.text: A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic Kaliningrad territory has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, Russian and Finnish authorities say.
The ship - the Sparta II - caught on fire after the strike on Saturday, and drifted into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said, adding: "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones were used, according to preliminary information, and that there is "no threat" to their supplies.
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and American governments.
The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011, and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.

On Saturday morning, Finnish defence forces detected the drone attack on the cargo vessel west of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland, which prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" over the area.
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".

A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship, and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."
The Finnish Border Guard also said the crew had not been forced to abandon the ship, no environmental damage had been detected, and there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.

articles.title: Suffolk village votes to ‘leave the UK’ over plans to house asylum seekers nearby
articles.summary:
Local MP says legitimate criticisms of asylum housing plans are being co-opted by opposition parties ‘stirring up racial discord’

Residents of a Suffolk village have voted to “leave the UK”…

blocks.text: Residents of a Suffolk village have voted to “leave the UK” in a referendum held in response to government plans to house 930 asylum seekers at a nearby former military base.
Approximately 500 people in Barnham were eligible to take part in the symbolic vote on Saturday. There were 257 votes for independence, 16 against and one spoiled ballot.
After the vote, Helen Beck, the chair of Barnham Residents’ Association, said Barnham’s flag would be a stone curlew on a “Suffolk blue background”.
RAF Barnham was one of three Ministry of Defence sites named in June by the government as potential locations for new developments to house asylum seekers.

blocks.caption: The flag of Barnham’s mooted new crown dependency, featuring a stone curlew against a ‘Suffolk blue background’.  Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty Images

blocks.text: A similar referendum was held in Piddington, Oxfordshire in September, with residents also voting to leave the UK amid plans to house more than 1,000 migrants at another former military base.

In Barnham, the plans have prompted protests outside the site. The referendum asked residents whether they supported seeking a “crown dependency status”, which is a similar system to that of Jersey, Guernsey and the Isle of Man.
John Bauer, the parish council chair, said this would allow the village to “retain loyalty to the crown” but remove itself from Home Office jurisdiction.

While in opposition the Labour party had attacked the Conservative policy to house asylum seekers on military bases; once in government, however, the party backtracked. The Conservatives have also reversed their position, with Kemi Badenoch telling frustrated villagers “the Conservative party is on your side”.
“We know that the problem of the boats needs to stop and we have got a plan to stop it,” she said on Friday.
Earlier this month, it was announced construction firm Kier would design the new camp at RAF Barnham.

Before Saturday’s vote Labour’s Dr Peter Prinsley, the local MP, said he was against the development of the site. Prinsley said the plans resembled a “concentration camp”, and warned that planning permission may be difficult to attain due to environmental concerns about rare species living in the area – in particular, stone curlews – with previous development applications nearby having been turned down.

“This is a symbolic referendum,” Prinsley said. “It’s not going to produce a binding result. I’m expecting that [the result] will be hugely in favour of becoming a crown dependency. There are 500 electors, so I’m expecting it to be 500 – nil.”
He added that the government “is doing an awful lot to deal with the irregular migration problem”, and highlighted that net migration may come down to “more or less zero by the end of the year”.

But he added that he didn’t think “the large army camps in remote locations are ever likely to be appropriate for the distribution of people seeking asylum. The fact is that people who arrive here on small boats are not illegal migrants. They are people who are seeking asylum. Our political opponents have described these people as ‘illegals, criminals, rapists’, and all sorts of things that they’re not. They’re just people who have arrived on small boats. The government is getting a grip on this problem, but it’s a complicated problem.”

He said the proposed Barnham site had particular issues which may make it unsuitable. “It’s a remote location without any pedestrian access, it’s on a very hazardous main road. When it was used as military accommodation there were serious accidents on that road.

“It’s also a site of special scientific interest because it is the nesting site for stone curlews, which will make any planning application very difficult – even a government planning application – because these are worldwide protections.”
He suggested “disused office blocks in some of the larger cities” may be more appropriate places to house asylum seekers, with more local services available.

blocks.caption: The permanent protest camp outside the gates of the former RAF base where the Home Office propose to house asylum seekers. Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty Images

blocks.text: “It feels like a concentration camp,” Prinsley added. “It doesn’t feel like a place that has a compassionate approach to people who are fleeing persecution and are being processed for asylum.”
He also said legitimate criticism of the plans had been co-opted by opposition parties who are aiming to “stir up racial discord”.
A Home Office spokesperson said: “We recognise the strength of feeling in local communities and are listening carefully to the concerns being raised.
“The government is working on a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country, with over £1bn saved in costs since the election.

“This includes closing all asylum hotels and moving to alternative accommodation, including former military sites. These are designed to be self-contained, with 24/7 security and CCTV, to reduce the impact on local communities.”

articles.title: Trump orders contractors to check with White House over any congressional inquiries
articles.summary:
Anticipating flood of Democratic requests, US president issues executive order in attempt to stymie oversight efforts

Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to…

blocks.text: Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to an executive order issued late Friday.

The companies must also coordinate with the White House and US agencies on “appropriate responses” to any such requests, the order says. If they fail to comply, the White House warns, their contracts could be terminated and their future work with the federal government suspended.

The order signed late Friday is the administration’s latest effort to resist what are expected to be wide-ranging and aggressive oversight efforts from Democrats when they take over Congress in January. Democrats have made government contracts one of their top investigative targets , noting that federal money has been flowing to companies linked with Trump’s family, particularly at the Pentagon.

It comes as White House officials have already begun taking steps to exert more control over how agencies and officials respond to congressional requests, anticipating there will be a flood of investigations once Democrats take power in January.

On Monday, Will Scharf, the White House counsel, told US agencies that they must seek approval from his office and the White House’s office of legislative affairs before agreeing to appear before Congress. Scharf also suggested in a recent letter to the US representative Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, that some congressional investigations may amount to “blatant criminality”.

Garcia earlier this week sent letters directing members of Trump’s family and top administration officials to preserve documents. Scharf sought to dismiss the requests, noting in a letter to Democratic lawmakers that they are not yet in the majority and cannot compel compliance.

In a fact sheet, the White House framed the new requirements as “protecting executive privileges from congressional overreach”, arguing that some congressional leaders have tried to intrude on executive branch privileges by “harassing private companies that contract with the federal government”.

Presidents of both parties have long used executive privilege to resist congressional inquiries, but the claims can set up messy, protracted legal fights as parties dispute whether it applies. Executive privilege allows the president to keep information from the courts, Congress and the public to protect the confidentiality of White House deliberations, but the protection is far from absolute.
Friday’s executive order applies to all contractors and subcontractors, a universe of tens of thousands of businesses.

articles.title: Alleged Mexican drug cartel boss ‘El Chapo Isidro’ arrested in special forces raid
articles.summary:
Fausto Isidro Meza Flores was one of FBI’s most wanted fugitives and evaded capture for more than a decade

The Mexican military captured one of the FBI’s top 10 most wanted fugitives during…

blocks.text: The Mexican military captured one of the FBI’s top 10 most wanted fugitives during a special forces raid in the Mexican state of Sinaloa on Friday night.
Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro”, was arrested along with two other alleged leaders of his gang after a gun battle that sparked widespread panic in the city of Guasave.

The alleged leader of a major drug-trafficking cartel, the Meza Flores Transnational Criminal Organization (TCO), he had managed to evade arrest for more than a decade, even though there was a reward of up to $5m (£3.8m) on his head.

blocks.caption: Video posted by Mexican authorities shows police leading man away

blocks.text: His FBI “most wanted” poster states his organisation “is allegedly responsible for the possession, distribution, and importation of large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl, and marijuana into the United States, and has predominately controlled drug production, transportation, and distribution in several locations throughout Mexico”.
Mexico’s defence ministry also alleged he is the leader of the Beltrán Leyva criminal organisation, which is allied to the Mayos, one of two rival factions in the powerful Sinaloa cartel.
Meza Flores’s alleged second-in-command, Germán N, whose alias is “Serafín”, and José N, an alleged financial operator for the Beltrán Leyva group, were also arrested.
The operation to capture the men was carried out by “elite military forces” with help from US intelligence, according to Mexico’s defence ministry.

After arriving in the “target area … using stealth and surprise”, the ministry said the arresting force came under attack “with gunfire and explosives” but managed to enter a house and make the arrests.
The men were then evacuated to Mexico City on a Mexican air force plane to be handed over to prosecutors.

blocks.caption: Meza Flores’s FBI ‘most wanted’ poster Photograph: FBI

blocks.text: Videos and photos show civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game at Kuroda Park stadium in Guasave, as well as burnt-out cars.

A barrage of rapid fire from what appeared to be Mexican security force helicopters fired at the ground, according to CNN, and players from the Venados de Mazatlán and Algodoneros de Guasave teams abandoned the field mid-game.
Meza Flores was originally indicted in 2012, and in 2013 the US Treasury placed sanctions on him under the Kingpin Act, freezing his assets.
In 2017, the US Department of State’s Narcotics Rewards Program began offering up to $5m as a reward for information leading directly to his arrest or conviction.
He has been charged with multiple counts of drug-trafficking violations and use and possession of a firearm in the US and was wanted in Mexico for organised crime and offences against public health.

articles.title: Hegseth reportedly moves to restrict defence ties with Canada, but Ottawa sees no change
articles.summary: A reported secret Pentagon directive restricting military co-operation with Canada has caught Ottawa off guard. Canadian defence officials say they've seen no evidence of restrictions taking effect.…

image.caption: U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth speaks to journalists at a military air base in Bogota, Colombia, on Wednesday. Hegseth has reportedly issued a classified directive restricting military co-operation between the U.S. and Canada. (Fernando Vergara/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

A reported secret Pentagon directive restricting military co-operation with Canada has caught Ottawa off guard. Canadian defence officials say they've seen no evidence of restrictions taking effect. The Pentagon insists NORAD, NATO and intelligence cooperation remain untouched, but questions persist about military exercises, training and broader bilateral defence planning.
Classified Pentagon directive raises questions about future Canada-U.S. military co-operation

U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has reportedly issued a classified directive restricting military co-operation between the United States and Canada — something that Canadian government and military officials were not aware of and have seen no evidence it has been put into practice.
The Washington Post reported late Friday that the directive was circulated last week in a secret memorandum. The report cited U.S. officials familiar with the decision.

Three Canadian defence officials speaking on background on Saturday said they were aware of the reports and were looking to substantiate them, as well as seeking clarification because there's been no change at the military operational level between the two countries.

Defence Minister David McGuinty, speaking to Reuters at the Halifax International Security Forum — where there is a large U.S. congressional delegation present — said the two countries continue to work "hand-in-glove" on various missions such as stopping the flow of illegal drugs in the Caribbean and on new policy initiatives such as integrated air and missile defence.
"I still see no daylight between what we're doing, military to military, and otherwise," McGuinty told Reuters.

Minister of National Defence David McGuinty rises during question period in the House of Commons on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Nov. 3. McGuinty says Canada and the U.S. continue to work 'hand-in-glove' on various military missions and new policy initiatives. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)
McGuinty is expected to meet with the bipartisan delegation of U.S. lawmakers later on Saturday in Halifax where the report is expected to be discussed.

There was no mention of the directive from the Americans at the security forum dinner Friday night, according to two of the confidential defence sources, one of whom wondered if the congressmen and senators were even aware of it.
CBC News is not identifying the sources because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
The existence of such a directive would only add to mounting tensions between the long-standing allies over trade and defence spending.
Canada, U.S. working on trade deal

The move comes as the Trump administration and the government of Prime Minister Mark Carney inch toward a trade deal that could see some relief in key sectors such as automotive and steel and aluminum.

The military and defence ties between Canada and the U.S. are deep, long-standing and would be difficult to restrict at an operational level without harming the security of the U.S. itself in one fashion or another, said one of the sources.

items: Dr. Strangelove diplomacy: How the Pentagon’s symbolic defence board freeze with Canada could backfire

blocks.text: The two countries co-operate in the defence of North America through NORAD. In Europe, they are founding partners of NATO and work side by side with the other 30 members of the Western alliance. They also work together in the Indo-Pacific in joint military exercises.

A third source said it would also be difficult and counter-productive for Washington to, for example, restrict access to U.S.-made weapons systems and equipment, which Washington has been eager to sell and pressuring Canada to buy.
Carney says he examined 'extreme tail risk' of U.S. military action in Canada

The scope of Hegseth's restrictions is unclear, according to the Washington Post report. Since the memo is classified, the Department of War has not identified which military programs or activities might be affected.

In a statement to CBC News, which was also shared with other media, the Pentagon's chief spokesperson, Sean Parnell, ruled out restrictions on operational level matters, but was vague on what precise impact the memo would have.

"The Department of War is taking steps to ensure its engagements with Canada advance tangible U.S. defence objectives and ultimately support a reinvigorated defence relationship," Parnell said in a written response.

items: Trump says he's working on a 'fair' trade deal with Canada
U.S. senator says Canada should make interim tariff agreement, let Congress 'legislate' long-term deal

blocks.text: "DoW is prioritizing opportunities for bilateral cooperation that strengthens the defence of our Homelands and shared hemisphere, while supporting Canada's ability to meet NATO obligations. This guidance does not impact defence intelligence co-operation, our binational NORAD command or our co-operation through NATO."
The response leaves questions about bilateral military exercises, training exchanges, defence planning and other forms of co-operation.
But even on that level, Canadian officials say they've seen no evidence thus far of any restrictions and point to the notion that the memo has been in circulation for a week.
Pentagon withdraws from Canada-U.S. defence board
Last spring, the Trump administration paused U.S. participation in the Permanent Joint Board on Defence (PJBD) with Canada.

Halting the activity of the decades-old board, a bilateral advisory group that co-ordinates continental security and recommends defence policy to both governments, was considered largely symbolic because it met infrequently.
Canada has been routinely criticized in Washington over its lacklustre defence spending.
There has been change under Carney, and Canada has now hit the NATO target of spending two per cent of GDP.

Carney, however, has publicly stated he wants to diversify both the country's trading relationship and where it sources its military equipment. He has said it's not good for more than 70 cents of defence equipment dollars to be going to one market — the United States.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.

articles.title: Montreal police arrest 2 ex-officers for alleged assault, criminal harassment, breach of trust
articles.summary: The two officers had previously been placed on administrative leave and then fired from the Montreal police service. They were arrested after Quebec's Crown prosecutor's office, the DPCP, issued a…

image.caption: Other related criminal investigations are still being handled by the SPVM's Division des normes professionnelles. (CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal·Breaking

The two officers had previously been placed on administrative leave and then fired from the Montreal police service. They were arrested after Quebec's Crown prosecutor's office, the DPCP, issued a warrant.
Arrests connected to allegations of discriminatory, racist acts by officers at Station 39

The Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) announced Saturday in a news release that it arrested two of its own officers in connection with allegations of discriminatory and racist acts by police officers at Station 39.
The arrested officers were released under the promise to return to court, where they will face charges of assault, criminal harassment and breach of trust, according to the SPVM.
The two officers had previously been placed on administrative leave, and were among seven police officers who were fired on Nov. 2.
Other related criminal investigations are still being handled by the SPVM's Division des normes professionnelles.
More to come.

articles.title: Vance stops short of endorsing Trump’s claim that Iran was close to nuclear weapon
articles.summary:
US vice-president says it’s not his place to second-guess the president, but refrains from endorsing Trump’s claim

At a White House news conference on Friday, JD Vance stopped short of…

blocks.text: At a White House news conference on Friday, JD Vance stopped short of endorsing Donald Trump’s claim that Iran was so close to obtaining a nuclear weapon in February that it was essential for the US to go to war with the Islamic republic.

In the White House briefing room, Trump was asked about reporting this week that he was unhappy with the US vice-president’s statement blaming Republican losses in the midterm elections on the Iran war.

“I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” Trump said. “I thought the statement was fine, except I would have had one other thing, that if it were asked, I would have said that: ‘Would you do it again?’ And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”

However, Trump’s claim that Iran was so close to developing a nuclear weapon this year that it was necessary to go to war, which he has made dozens of times in the past nine months, is undermined by public evidence and contradicts his own previous statements on US strikes against Iranian facilities in 2025.
At a campaign rally in Alaska last month, Trump insisted that he had to join Israel in attacking Iran in February because, “they were two weeks away from having a nuclear weapon”.

That claim appears at odds with what his then director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, testified to Congress on 25 March 2025, two months into Trump’s second term: that US intelligence agencies reported that Iran had not tried to make a nuclear weapon for more than two decades. The US intelligence community, Gabbard said, “continues to assess Iran is not building a nuclear weapon and supreme leader Khamenei has not authorized the nuclear weapons program he suspended in 2003”.

Despite that assessment, three months later, on 21 June 2025, Trump ordered the US bombing of Iran’s nuclear enrichment facilities. The strikes, Trump told the public that night, “were a spectacular military success. Iran’s key nuclear enrichment facilities have been completely and totally obliterated.”

Eight months after that, however, when Trump announced the start of a full-scale war on Iran early on 28 February 2026, he said in a video statement from Mar-a-Lago the war was necessary to “ensure that Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon”.
The morning after this month’s midterm elections, Vance said in a statement posted on social media: “The reason we lost is the war.”

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” he added. “Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost.”

In the White House briefing room on Friday, after Trump said that Vance should have said the war was necessary, a reporter asked the vice-president whether he would argue that the war in Iran was worth it.

In his response, Vance said it was not his place to second-guess the president, but refrained from actually endorsing Trump’s claim that the war was essential to stop Iran from creating a nuclear weapon.

“Look, what I’ve said is the goal of keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon is absolutely what we need to be doing. It’s the biggest state sponsor of terrorism. If they had a nuclear weapon, they would use it as leverage or, God forbid, they would attack and kill thousands, hundreds of thousands, of innocent people,” Vance said. “I think the president is the one who makes the decision, and the president has said he would do it again.”
“My view is that my goal is, and my job is, to support the president of the United States,” the vice-president said.
The vice president’s office did not respond to a request to comment.

articles.title: Russian helicopter suspected of violating Finnish airspace
articles.summary: Finland's Defense Ministry thinks the incursion is linked to a drone strike earlier Saturday on a Russian cargo ship, which is on a US sanctions list.

image.caption: Finnish fighter jets were scrambled after a similar incident in Estonian airspace in September 2025Image: Forsvarsmakten/AFP

blocks.text: A Russian helicopter is suspected of violating Finnish airspace, the Nordic country's Ministry of Defense said Saturday.
The incident happened a few hours after a drone attack left a Russian cargo ship ablaze in the Gulf of Finland, the easternmost part of the Baltic Sea.
What do we know?
According to Finland's Defense Ministry, the incursion happened at 12:34 p.m. local time (10:34 UTC/GMT) off the town of Loviisa, on the southern coast.

"This alleged airspace violation may be linked to rescue or surveillance operations carried out by Finland following damage sustained by a cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland," public broadcaster YLE cited Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen as saying.
The ministry added the helicopter could have penetrated up to 4.1 kilometers (2.5 miles) into Finnish territory.

blocks.caption: The Finnish Defense Ministry said there is no further danger to shipping or the publicImage: Antti Hämäläinen/Lehtikuva/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What do we know about the cargo ship attack?

Earlier Saturday, Finland — one of NATO's newest members — said a Russian cargo ship heading for Russia's Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad caught fire after being struck by drones in the Gulf of Finland.
The Finnish military said the Sparta II was damaged ⁠west ⁠of Russia's Gogland island, about 40 kilometers (25 miles) from Finland's coast, and later drifted into Finnish territorial waters.
Finnish ‌Border ​Guard Commander Ilja Iljin later told YLE that the vessel, which is known to have links to the Russian military, was struck by Ukrainian drones while in Russian waters.
"At the moment, ​there is no confirmed information ⁠about ​what cargo ​is on board, ​but it ‌cannot be ruled out ​that ⁠there is military materiel on ⁠board," ​Iljin said.
The ship is on a US sanctions list, according to a search of the Open Sanctions website.
The Border Guard later said the crew of the Sparta II was evacuating into a life raft and rescue boat.

blocks.caption: Finland's Prime Minister Petteri Orpo is concerned about the Ukraine war spilloverImage: Virginia Mayo/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Orpo backs Ukraine against 'aggressor'
"The [Ukraine] war is spilling over into our neighbouring areas," wrote Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo on X.
Ukraine has the right to fight against the aggressor," he added.

articles.title: Anthropic mathematician claims he used Claude to prove 19th-century Riemann hypothesis
articles.summary:
Levent Alpöge says it took six weeks for him using the AI tool to solve the math problem involving prime numbers

A mathematician at

blocks.text: A mathematician at Anthropic is contending that the San Francisco-based artificial intelligence (AI) company’s software has helped crack one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.

Levent Alpöge, a Turkish American mathematician, on Friday posted a note on his personal website saying that Claude, the AI software, had helped prove the Riemann hypothesis. He says that Claude helped develop a solution to the problem during the course of about six weeks.

If Alpöge’s claim is ultimately confirmed, the proof could mark another breakthrough in the use of AI for complicated math problems – even as mathematicians express uneasiness around extremely lucrative private companies dishing out millions of dollars for the technology to solve problems.

“Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line,” Alpöge wrote, while anthropomorphizing the AI software. “No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”
Alpöge linked to computer code – written in a language called Lean – that he maintained could verify the findings.
Mathematicians subsequently began working to see if Alpöge’s proof could be confirmed.

Alpöge’s note was published just one day after Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq stock market index. He acknowledged that, writing: “The precise timing is horrible. If I could have, I’d have finished this all much earlier.”
The Riemann hypothesis is a nearly 170-year-old math problem named after Bernhard Riemann, a German mathematician who proposed it in 1859.

The hypothesis deals with prime numbers – whole numbers greater than 1 that can only be divided by themselves and 1. Riemann questioned how often prime numbers appear and how they are distributed along the number line. And he developed a formula for estimating how many prime numbers exist under a specific number.
The Riemann hypothesis is one of the seven Millennium prize math problems selected in 200 by the Clay Mathematics Institute. The institute has offered $1m for each problem solved.

Mathematicians have been attempting to solve this problem for years. The New York Times reported that on Friday, an independent mathematician in Italy released an incomplete proof of the Riemann hypothesis that he said he had been working on for almost 12 years. That mathematician, Alessandro Masullo, said he did not use AI because he did not fully trust the system.
after newsletter promotion
Other mathematicians have expressed discomfort with relying on AI to solve math problems.

In September, Anthropic competitor OpenAI claimed that a non-public version of its AI tools helped solve part of another Millennium prize problem. But it was solved in a way that struck mathematicians and observers in a way many found strange: a near-trillion-dollar private company spent $15m to employ 10,000 AI systems to solve the problem.
Alpöge was working on that separate problem for Anthropic when OpenAI made its announcement.

University of Warwick mathematician James Robinson told the Guardian in September that “it’s frustrating to see these big tech companies burning this fuel up just so that they can show off about how great their latest model is”.

He added: “It seems like immature playground boasting writ large, underpinned by billions of dollars and the potential for significant environmental damage in an age when climate change is probably the biggest challenge we face.”

articles.title: International UN talks on controlling use of autonomous weapons collapse
articles.summary:
Week-long efforts fail to establish negotiating mandate on AI warfare after Russian ‘filibustering’

Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international…
articles.byline: Frances Mao in Geneva and Patrick Wintour

blocks.text: Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am after all-night talks failed to overcome Russian objections.

Despite an overwhelming majority of states at the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) in Geneva wanting to agree a negotiating mandate leading to a legally binding treaty, the need for consensus forced the conference to adopt a much weaker option.
The mandate asked countries “to elaborate by consensus”, an instrument that may not carry any legal obligations.

Although Russia led the objections using obstructive stalling tactics, other military powers invested in AI warfare, such as the US, were reluctant to commit to a legally binding protocol protecting civilians from robot drones and other autonomous weapons.

blocks.caption: Delegates attend the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons in Geneva. Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: Some argued that international humanitarian law was sufficient. More than 100 states had been pushing for a new law, saying the weapons raised entirely new challenges. European and Nato states, including Ukraine, China and Iran, expressed support or willingness for a new protocol.

The US said the need for human control over autonomous weapons had been discussed at the Apec summit in meetings between president Xi Jinping and Donald Trump this week, but the US was reluctant to agree a binding treaty.

South Korea, Japan, Turkey, the UK, France and Germany were among the defence tech powers exploring AI-enabled weapons who also expressed resistance to being bound by a new law, instead advocating for a nonbinding agreement.

The CCW is a UN forum that operates via consensus, meaning all 128 parties to the convention have to agree unanimously to pass a statement. The high threshold has resulted in the CCW failing to pass any new laws regulating weapons in the past 30 years and states seeking pathways elsewhere to pass treaties, such as the 2008 ban on cluster munitions.

The Future of Life Institute’s chair, Max Tegmark, said world leaders had failed to meet the moment this week. “Slaughterbots are already here,” he said. “Yet states have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about this for the 14th year.”

blocks.caption: A campaign billboard is driven past the Houses of Parliament in London calling for control of AI weapons. Photograph: Andy Rain/EPA

blocks.text: Diplomats inside the negotiations said Russia had been deliberately filibustering and not working in good faith, as opposed to the US delegates, who had been seeking a path to reach a consensus statement.

The exclusion of several nonmember countries from negotiations also prompted a rare protest in the chamber on the final day of the conference, with the Egyptian delegation shouting at the conference chair.
after newsletter promotion

Israel and the US have also used AI-enabled targeting systems to conduct tens of thousands of strikes in Gaza and Iran, which have resulted in mass casualties. The Pentagon struck more than 1,000 targets in Iran on the first day of the war, and according to investigative media reports, the US military is aiming to carry out 1,000 AI-assisted targeting decisions per hour.

Critics said this outcome was a missed opportunity, noting that states had been discussing the issue of autonomous weapons, their dangers, and the need for international rules on how to restrict and regulate them for 13 years and large substantive parts of a treaty had already been settled upon.
One European diplomat said: “There was no political will to really regulate these weapons. No will commensurate to the urgency and need.”

A Human Rights Watch’s senior arms adviser, Bonnie Docherty, who had been directly involved in previously successful treaties banning cluster munitions and nuclear weapons, said autonomous weapons needed binding law. She noted that treaties could be negotiated within 15 months and dismissed the US’s proposal of five years to sort out a mandate.
A bloc of seven countries – Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama – had led the push for a binding treaty to be negotiated within one year.

On Wednesday Brazil’s delegate told the floor: “These are not weapons of the future being discussed here, these are already in use and being further developed. We are late in developing these norms and rules to regulate these lethal autonomous weapons systems.”

Violence and shows of force by cartels are common following the capture or killing of leaders. (Yohar

blocks.text: World·New
Mexican authorities captured top cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as El Chapo Isidro, in the state of Sinaloa overnight, resulting in a burst of violence that rattled civilians.
Fausto Isidro Meza Flores was a key ally for a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel known as Los Mayos

The government said in a report early Saturday that intelligence from the United States helped with the capture of Meza Flores, but provided few details about how authorities in Mexico and the U.S. co-ordinated to detain him.

Meza Flores was one of the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives and a top cartel leader from the Beltrán Leyva criminal organization, and was a key ally for a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel known as Los Mayos. His capture represents a blow to the cartel as it fights with another faction for control of the northern Mexican state.

Images from the city of Guasave, where Meza Flores was captured, show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, burning cars and gas stations, and circling helicopters shooting at homes below. Such shows of force by cartels are common following the capture or killing of leaders.

items: Mexico made 'high-risk bet' in taking down cartel boss El Mencho

blocks.text: Meza Flores was wanted for trafficking drugs to the U.S. and illegally carrying firearms. The U.S. government didn't immediately provide more details or comment on the detention.
Vehicles on fire on a highway near Los Mochis, Sinaloa, on Friday following the announcement of El Chapo Isidro's arrest. (Yohari Leon/Facebook/Reuters)

Mexican authorities said they used "stealth and surprise" to capture him, establishing a security perimeter around the building where he was located. Upon being attacked with guns and explosives from likely cartel operatives, armed forces personnel entered a home and detained Meza Flores, they said.
Video shared by authorities shows heavily armed men in camouflage marching a man who appears to be Meza Flores through a dimly lit house and putting him in the back of a truck.

The high-profile capture comes as Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum faces pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump to crack down on cartels. Sheinbaum has gone after illegal groups more aggressively than her predecessors, and homicides have dipped significantly in her two years in office.
Thousands stuck in Mexico as cartel chaos calms

Her government has immobilized a number of cartel kingpins. Chief among them was Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as El Mencho, who was killed in February. Similar to the capture of Meza Flores, the dramatic operation resulted in a burst of violence and burning cars.

items: Families of Canadian mining firm workers kidnapped in Mexico plan to file RCMP complaint

blocks.text: Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch wrote in a post on X on Saturday morning that armed forces would remain deployed in Sinaloa to protect civilians.
"These detentions are an important step in pacifying Sinaloa," he said.

articles.title: ‘Philippines to buy 100% of farm products, energy from US’
articles.summary: The Philippines has agreed to buy all its agricultural and energy requirements from the US, President Donald Trump said days after his bilateral meeting with President Marcos, who had emphasized the…

blocks.text: November 22, 2026 | 12:00am
Trump invokes Philippines -US security relations

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines has agreed to buy all its agricultural and energy requirements from the US, President Donald Trump said days after his bilateral meeting with President Marcos, who had emphasized the need for the country to have diverse sources of supply of commodities.
Trump said the Philippines was buying a lot of its farm products from other countries, including Brazil, prompting him to ask Marcos to source all its agricultural needs from the US.

“And the Philippines, as you know, was buying a lot of their farm product from other countries, including Brazil, much more than from us. And I said, here’s the deal, you buy 100 percent of your agriculture from January 1st from our farmers,” he told reporters at the White House yesterday (Philippine time).

“We’re the greatest farmers in the world with the greatest equipment in the world. You know, we support these countries, but they don’t buy from us. So I said, you are going to buy 100 percent of your farm product, not 90, not 95,” he added.
At a media interview in China on Friday, Marcos admitted the two countries would like to finalize a trade deal, but there was no mention of buying all of the Philippines’ requirements from the US.
According to Trump, the Philippines would be buying “billions and billions of dollars” of farm products from the US.

“Is Brazil going to help them in case they get into a little skirmish with China? I don’t think so. They buy from Brazil and other countries, and now they’re buying from us 100 percent, not 99 percent,” the US president said.

“They buy it mostly from the Middle East. Can you believe it?” he added. “I said, ‘If China attacks you, is the Middle East going to come to your rescue?’ ‘No, sir.’ ‘Well, that’s good. Don’t buy from them anymore.”

Marcos and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva held a bilateral meeting in the Philippines last Nov. 14 to discuss ways to boost partnership in renewable energy and biofuels, livestock production and animal health, modern farming, education, science and technology, law enforcement and other fields.
Trump claimed the Philippines would also purchase 100 percent of its energy requirements from the US.

“Also, energy, they buy 20 percent from us, but they buy – I said, where do you get your energy? I was with Prime Minister Marcos, who’s a very good man, by the way. Great family. But I said, where do you buy your energy? Should we buy it from the Middle East? I said, not anymore, you don’t,” he said, erroneously referring to the President as prime minister.
“You’re going to buy 100 percent of your energy from us, yes, sir. So instead of having a deficit, we have a huge – I could do this with every country.”
Diversified sources
In China last Friday, Marcos said the Philippines needs to diversify its sources of key commodities, emphasizing that nothing was discussed about buying all of Manila’s requirements from Washington.

“The trade deal is a response to the tariff schedule that the US tried to impose. They imposed it but it was struck down in court. But anyway, it still brought open the question of the trade between the US and the Philippines,” Marcos said.
“And it is timely because the Philippines, as you know, is looking for many, many, many ways to expand, to diversify our sources of supply of different commodities,” he added.
Marcos said the conflict between Russia and Ukraine highlighted the need for the Philippines to find new trade partners.

“We are continuing to open new partners to engage, new engagements, to have new engagements, to have new partnerships with everybody around the world. So that the way I put it is that if you’re standing on one foot, if you rely on just one party, it would be prone to problems. If you rely on several parties, even if one of them encounters problems, you can run to the others,” the President said.
“And that’s why the trade deal is important. And we are proposing to buy more agricultural products for one thing,” he added.
The negotiations, Marcos said, covered more purchases of farm products from the US, including soybeans and wheat.
“We are looking for cheaper sources of food products. We are looking for cheaper sources for energy importation. And that is – the bulk of our discussion with President Trump was that,” he said.

“So there is the trade deal, which is the result of the tariff schedule that the US attempted to impose, but nonetheless opened the discussion on trade. And there was the specific on energy and agricultural products during the meeting with President Trump.”
A White House statement said Trump has also announced the Philippines’ commitment to “eliminate the US trade deficit with the Philippines.” — Louella Desidero

articles.title: Duterte camp to ICC: Exclude recorded testimony of ex-DDS
articles.summary: The defense team of former president Rodrigo Duterte has urged the trial judges of the International Criminal Court (ICC) to exclude the recorded testimony of a former police officer who claimed to…

blocks.text: Headlines
November 22, 2026 | 12:00am
Photos courtesy of the International Criminal Court show former president Rodrigo Duterte during his first in-person appearance before the tribunal since his arrest in March 2025.
Photos / ICC | via Janvic Mateo

MANILA, Philippines — The defense team of former president Rodrigo Duterte has urged the trial judges of the International Criminal Court (ICC) to exclude the recorded testimony of a former police officer who claimed to be a former member of the so-called Davao death squad (DDS).
In a 12-page filing dated Nov. 18, defense lawyer Peter Haynes opposed the prosecution’s request to admit the prior recorded testimony of the witness identified as “P-0002.”
The prosecution, in its original request, described the witness as a former Davao City Police officer who was part of the death squad.

“P-0002’s evidence supports the existence of a policy to neutralize alleged criminals in Davao City, as shown by, (i) the provision of financial incentives; (ii) the use of State and civilian forces and (iii) the dissemination of this policy by Mr. Duterte to the perpetrators,” read the Nov. 5 filing of acting prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang.

Niang requested the Trial Chamber III to allow the recorded testimony of the witness as he is no longer available to testify during the trial. It was unclear why the witness is no longer available to testify.
According to Haynes, admitting P-0002’s recorded testimony would be prejudicial to Duterte as the defense would not be able to cross examine him during trial proceedings.
“P-0002’s statement contains repeated references to Mr. Duterte’s acts and conduct, on which the prosecution places heavy reliance in its trial brief,” the defense lawyer said.
These include allegations on Duterte’s supposed role in establishing the death squad, as well as direct orders to commit various crimes.
Haynes also questioned the probative value of the recorded testimony, claiming that P-0002 is an unreliable witness.
ICC case strong
Former United Nations special rapporteur on extrajudicial executions Agnès Callamard is confident the ICC will convict Duterte for crimes against humanity.
Callamard, now secretary general of Amnesty International, told The STAR on Friday there is enough evidence to establish Duterte’s role in the alleged crimes.

“Sadly for ex-president Duterte, he has left behind much evidence of his commitment to killings. He has made many public statements. He has called for others to kill. He has demanded killings. He has done so over and over and over again,” he said.

“It’s not about the number of cases. It is about demonstrating the organized nature of the killings, and I suspect that the International Criminal Court has all the evidence that it needs,” she added.
Despite the ongoing proceedings at The Hague, Callamard maintained the Philippine government still has a lot to do to ensure that all victims attain justice.
“Handing over Duterte to the International Criminal Court was a good thing, but it is not enough. They now need to take a step to tackle the culture of impunity within the Philippines,” she said.

articles.title: Gatchalian lauds JV for weeding out P97 billion ‘non-compliant’ projects
articles.summary: Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian lauded finance committee chairman Sen. JV Ejercito for being stricter than him in handling the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027, which saw P97.5…

blocks.text: November 22, 2026 | 12:00am
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian and Senator JV Ejercito
The Philippine STAR / Ryan Baldemor

MANILA, Philippines — Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian lauded finance committee chairman Sen. JV Ejercito for being stricter than him in handling the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027, which saw P97.5 billion in public works projects excised for being non-compliant.
Speaking to radio dzMM yesterday, Gatchalian said he also removed questionable budget items when he was finance committee chair that scrutinized the 2026 national budget.

While technical descriptions were required last year, the finance committee now under Ejercito is requiring more documentation, like programs of works, certificates of implementability, Regional Development Council approval and correct geotagging coordinates.
Gatchalian said his own research flagged 295 public works projects worth P8.836 billion based on the executive’s spending plan, the National Expenditure Program.
He was shocked that the current finance committee weeded out up to P97.5 billion in noncompliant projects under the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH)’s proposed outlay.
“From P8.8 billion to P90-plus billion. I was surprised how strict Senator JV is. When he gives a deadline, finished or not finished, pass your paper,” Gatchalian said.
“And that’s correct. What we started in 2026 has become stricter,” he added.
Gatchalian welcomed the Senate move to reverse the cuts in foreign-assisted projects (FAPs) done by the House of Representatives in the latter’s version of the General Appropriations Bill (GAB).
Among the projects with restored government counterpart funding are the Metro Manila Subway, North-South Commuter Railway, Cavite-Bataan bridge and the Laguna Lakeshore road network.
“There’s a big difference between the Senate committee report and House GAB. The foreign-assisted projects were restored. The Senate rule now is no supporting documents, no budget,” Gatchalian said.
He said the finance committee under Ejercito will sponsor the budget tomorrow, signaling the start of marathon plenary debates on different agencies’ proposed budgets.

Gatchalian vowed that the Senate would finish its plenary debates in record time to pass the budget on final reading and immediately hold a bicameral conference committee meeting with the House to reconcile their conflicting GAB versions, to meet its target of ratifying the budget before Dec. 17 or the session adjournment.

articles.title: PPP plans for 9 airports, railway projects bared
articles.summary: Nine regional airports across the country are being readied for development under public-private partnership arrangement by next year, Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon announced on Friday.

blocks.text: November 22, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Nine regional airports across the country are being readied for development under public-private partnership (PPP) arrangement by next year, Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon announced on Friday.
The airports eyed for PPP are in Davao, Siargao, Bicol, Iloilo, Bacolod, Puerto Princesa, Busuanga, General Santos and Tacloban.

Speaking at the Stratbase Institute’s Pilipinas Conference 2026, Dizon said the Department of Transportation (DOTr) would begin with a bundled PPP covering the airports in Davao, Siargao and Bicol, which is expected to be awarded in the first quarter of 2027. The proposal, submitted by the group operating the Clark International Airport, is an unsolicited offer covering the development and operation of the three airports.

Dizon, who assumed his post after a Cabinet reshuffle earlier this month, said these projects were part of the administration’s broader push to finish infrastructure projects that had been stalled for years.

“(When he started), the President said that PPPs are the most important legacy that the President, this administration, is going to leave behind. And today, for airports, we have already privatized the most PPPs that any other administration has... nine airports will be PPPed by the time the President exits in June of 2028,” he said.
“That will really change the way our airports are run,” he added.
The DOTr, he added, will also pursue solicited PPPs for the Iloilo airport in the first half of 2027, followed by Bacolod, Puerto Princesa, Busuanga, General Santos and Tacloban airports.
Dizon said the administration had already pursued the PPP model for three airports, including the Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA), as well as the Bohol and Bicol airports.
Aside from airports, the DOTr is also preparing PPP arrangement for three major Metro Manila railway systems.

These include the Light Rail Transit Line 2 (LRT-2) and the Metro Rail Transit Line 3 (MRT-3). The department is also planning a PPP for the automated fare collection system covering the country’s major railway networks, including the Metro Manila Subway and the North-South Commuter Railway.

The solicited PPP for LRT-2, with assistance from the International Finance Corp. of the World Bank, and the MRT-3 project, with support from the Asian Development Bank, are targeted for completion next year.
Dizon also announced the opening before Christmas of the Cavite-Laguna Expressway (CALAX), which is 97 percent complete.
The first phase of the Toll Road 4 (TR4), connecting Laguna to Lucena, is expected to open early next year.
Stratbase Institute president Dindo Manhit said the investments are important, especially after the Philippines concluded its 2026 chairship of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

“The true measure of our ASEAN leadership will not simply be the meetings convened, declarations adopted or initiatives launched. It will be the partnerships we sustain, the opportunities we create and the regional priorities we continue to champion long after our chairship has ended,” Manhit said in his speech.
He stressed that economic initiatives must respond to the everyday concerns of Filipino households, including affordable necessities, employment and reliable public services.
“Filipinos want an economy that works for them. They want affordable necessities, decent jobs, reliable public services and opportunities to improve their lives,” he said.

Manhit said strategic partnerships, including initiatives such as the Luzon Economic Corridor involving the Philippines, the United States and Japan, must translate into investments, stronger industries and better-paying jobs.
“Our strategic partnerships must deliver results that Filipinos can feel – not just opportunities that look good on paper,” he said.

articles.title: Virginia child dies in state’s first measles-associated death of 2026
articles.summary:
Death adds to national measles outbreak that recently cost the US its measles elimination status after 26 years

Virginia reported…

blocks.text: Virginia reported its first measles-associated death of 2026 ⁠on Friday, involving a child who tested positive for the infectious disease, the state’s health department said.
The department said the child was ⁠age four or younger. It did not disclose additional details, including the child’s vaccination status, citing the family’s privacy.
The death adds to a worsening national measles outbreak that recently cost the US its measles elimination status after 26 years.
Pennsylvania, the hardest-hit US state, reported an eighth measles-related death and confirmed 1,631 measles cases as of Friday.
Wisconsin has ⁠also reported two deaths, while New York state recorded its first measles-associated ​death, involving a ​child.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has confirmed six ​measles-associated deaths so far in 2026, though it does not ​specify the states ‌where the deaths were ​recorded.

A discrepancy between ​state and federal death tallies arose after the CDC, under the Trump administration’s health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, began using National Center for Health Statistics mortality data instead of state figures.
Virginia has reported 220 measles ⁠cases so far in 2026, including 40 among children four years old or younger and 75 among those age five to 12, state ⁠health department data showed as of Thursday.
Of those cases, 179 involved unvaccinated individuals, 39 were associated with people ‌whose vaccination status was ‌unknown and two occurred with vaccinated individuals.

“Virginia has not had a measles-related death ‌since 1978,” said Frederic Bertley, immunologist and chief executive officer of the Center of Science and Industry. Bertley added that the measles virus infection is both alarming and evidence that measles is gaining a foothold and becoming a growing problem for the US.

Virginia health officials have reported increased measles activity driven largely by outbreaks ‌in the state’s central region. Buckingham county has reported 127 cases, the most in the state, while neighboring Charlotte county has recorded 34 ​cases.

articles.title: EU and Indonesia sign trade deal
articles.summary: A deal covering 730 million people promises lower tariffs and new investment opportunities as the European Union seeks to diversify trade ties amid growing global economic tensions.

image.caption: Palm oil exports are part of the deal but will be closely regulatedImage: Willy Kurniawan/REUTERS

blocks.text: The European Union and Indonesia signed a free trade deal on Saturday, describing it as a new chapter in economic relations between the two sides.
"This is one of the most ambitious deals the European Union has concluded in Asia," Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, said at the signing ceremony on Saturday.
"Together, we represent a market of 730 million people," she added.

The Indonesia-European Union Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) and the additional Investment Protection Agreement (IPA) are designed to reduce trade barriers and attract investment in strategic sectors such as electric vehicles, electronics, and pharmaceuticals.
The agreement comes after almost 10 years of negotiations and is part of a wider series of trade deals by the EU.
'Keeping the doors open when others are closing theirs'
The bloc hopes to reduce its reliance on individual economic partners as trade with both China and the US has become more difficult in recent years.
Von der Leyen also stressed the importance of international cooperation, saying that "in a time when others are closing their doors, we keep ours open."

blocks.caption: In 2025, von der Leyen met with Indonesian President Pabowo Subianto to work on the agreementImage: Laily Rachev - Biro Pers Sekretariat Presiden

blocks.text: The deal sees tariffs on about 98% of EU exports to Indonesia to be done away with. The EU estimates that European companies could save more than €600 million (around €658 million) per year.

"The benefits for our exporters are concrete and measurable," Indonesian Minister of Economic Affairs Airlangga Hartarto said, hailing a "new chapter" in economic relations with the EU. He said the deal would benefit his country’s main exports to Europe, including palm oil, footwear and textiles.

Palm oil and deforestation had been major stumbling blocks during the negotiations, and the agreement includes mechanisms for cooperation on regulatory and sustainability issues as well as a dedicated protocol on palm oil to address environmental concerns.
The EU parliament is now expected to greenlight the deal while Indonesian authorities will also complete the ratification process so it can enter into force in 2027.

articles.title: New EU budget proposal aims at tax gobal tech giants
articles.summary: European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a smaller EU budget for 2028-2034, including a 3% tax on major digital firms to ease member states' contributions. France has already rejected…

image.caption: Costa says he is "confident that this proposal is a good basis for moving towards a final agreement" Image: Christopher Katsarov/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a new draft for the next EU budget.
Among other things, he is suggesting a tax on big tech firms to ease the contributions of member states, some of which strongly criticised earlier proposals.
The EU budget is theEuropean Union’s shared budget and it is used for things ranging from agricultural subsidies, infrastructure projects to border control and defence.

A first draft for the 2028 to 2034 budget was proposed by the EU Commission in 2025 but was criticised, especially by a group of northern European members including Germany who wanted the budget to be much smaller.
Following that criticism, the European Council President has now suggested a new draft, which is smaller by €204 billion.
But divisions among member states appear to remain, with France immediately coming out against Costa’s new draft, saying it was "deeply disappointing."

blocks.caption: The EU budget also covers financial aid for UkraineImage: Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: What’s the plan for the tech tax?

The proposal includes a string of new "revenue channels," explicitly intended to "to keep national contributions at a reasonable level," so that member state will have to contribute less than otherwise would be the case.
The biggest splash would likely come from a tax on companies with an annual turnover from digital activities of at least 50 million euros in the EU and 750 million euros worldwide.

Those firms would be subject to "an annual contribution corresponding to 3% of the annual net turnover from online advertising, digital intermediation services and user-generated data," according to Costa.
Aside from the tech tax, the "balanced basket of new own resources" also includes taxes on tobacco products and electronic waste.
What happens next?

Neither the EU Commission nor European Council President Costa will have the final word on the budget. Costa's plan will now be at the centre of hours of talks when EU leaders meet in Brussels next week.

"This is a realistic budget that addresses our new priorities while preserving our established policies," Costa wrote about his proposal. "I am confident that this proposal is a good basis for moving towards a final agreement."
But an initial reaction from France suggests that any final agreement might still be some way off.
The French presidency said the budget "falls well short ​of ‌what is needed, particularly on ‌the Common Agricultural Policy, ‌notably ​to guarantee income support for farmers."
"As it ⁠stands, ​this proposal ​from the President ​of the European ‌Council does not ​provide ⁠a basis for an ⁠agreement."
The EU was hoping to reach a general agreement on the budget by the end of 2026 with its formal adoption planned for 2027.

articles.title: Russia strikes Zelenskyy's hometown, killing 2
articles.summary: The attacks follow Russian President Vladimir Putin's vow of a "painful" response to Ukraine's attacks this week on the Kerch Bridge, linking Russian-occupied Crimea.

image.caption: Kryvyi Rih is Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometownImage: Press service of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Russian ballistic missile strikes on Ukraine's southern city of Kryvyi Rih — President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown — killed two people and wounded dozens of others, local officials said Saturday.

The attacks come amid little progress in talks to end the nearly five-year-old war and after Ukraine, on three occasions this week, struck the Kerch bridge linking Russian-occupied Crimea with Russia.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had vowed a "painful" response to the Kerch attack, as the bridge is vital for war supplies for Russian forces in the south.
Russia intensifies aerial attacks on Ukraine
What do we know?
Among the dead in Friday evening's double-tap strikes on Kryvyi Rih were a 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman, while several children were among the 60 wounded, the Ukrainian officials said.

Several fires broke out and damage was caused to about 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools and an industrial facility, Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of the city administration, wrote on Telegram.
Moscow, meanwhile, confirmed a further strike on Friday night in Kryvyi Rih.
Russia's Defense Ministry said a thermal power plant in the city was hit, along with a power substation in the region of Rivne, on the opposite side of the country.
Both facilities supply electricity to the industry supporting Ukraine's military, the ministry added.

blocks.caption: Kryvyi Rih has been hit several times by Russia during the warImage: Press service of the National Police of Ukraine/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: What are the other latest developments?
Elsewhere in the nearly five-year-long war, Russia ​also struck a ​cargo vessel ‌near Odesa, which Moscow said was carrying dual-use goods ​for ⁠the Ukrainian military.
Eleven people, including two children, were wounded when a Russian drone attacked a five-story apartment building in the northeastern Kharkiv region, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said Saturday.
One person was wounded in a Russian attack on the capital, Kyiv, according to the service.
In Russia, local officials said Saturday that Ukrainian drone attacks wounded three people in the Bryansk and Belgorod border regions.

Finland, meanwhile, said it detected a drone attack on Saturday morning on a Russian cargo ship in the eastern Baltic Sea, prompting Prime Minister Petteri Orpo to warn that the war is "spilling over into our immediate vicinity."
After damage to Russia's Kerch bridge to Crimea, Zelenskyy warned in an interview with US broadcaster NBC that the structure "will not remain standing anyway."

articles.title: Princess of Wales speaks about impact of cancer diagnosis in BBC film Heal
articles.summary:
Documentary records Catherine taking on Three Peaks challenge and finding ‘sense of hope alongside uncertainty’

The Princess of Wales has spoken candidly about the impact of her cancer…

blocks.text: The Princess of Wales has spoken candidly about the impact of her cancer diagnosis in a BBC documentary to be aired later this month.

“Cancer does change you,” Catherine, 44, says in the trailer for the 30-minute programme. “It changes your body. It changes you physically, but there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.”

The film records Catherine taking on the Three Peaks challenge – climbing the three highest mountains in England, Scotland and Wales in 24 hours – and meeting with other people undergoing cancer treatment. Described by the BBC as a “highly personal film”, the documentary, titled Heal, will be shown on BBC One on 29 November.

blocks.caption: The Princess of Wales climbing Yr Wydffa in Snowdonia. Photograph: BBC/Kensington Palace/Matt Porteous

blocks.text: The trailer emerged as it was reported that King Charles will voluntarily pay “mansion tax” on relevant royal household properties, despite Crown exemption. The high-value council tax surcharge – often referred to as a mansion tax – will take effect in 2028 and apply to properties valued at more than £2m.
Catherine was diagnosed with an undisclosed form of cancer in early 2024, for which she received chemotherapy, and by January 2025 announced she was in remission.

She was treated at the Royal Marsden hospital in London, a world-leading oncology centre, with funds from the distribution of the documentary, which will also be broadcast in other countries, going to the Royal Marsden cancer charity.

When people successfully finish cancer treatment at the hospital they often ring a bell in celebration. “I didn’t ring the bell,” Catherine says in the trailer, speaking to her brothe, James Middleton as they are walking together.
“Maybe this is your ringing the bell,” he says, in reference to her undertaking the Three Peaks challenge and making the programme.

When she completed the challenge in June, 18 months after announcing that the cancer was in remission, she became the first royal to have achieved the feat – climbing Ben Nevis, Scafell Pike and Yr Wyddfa in less than 24 hours, having started on a Saturday evening.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Funds from the distribution of the film will go to the Royal Marsden cancer charity where Catherine was treated. Photograph: BBC/Kensington Palace/Matt Porteous

blocks.text: In the programme, which will be introduced by the presenter Kirsty Young, Catherine talks about how she has learned through her recovery to find “a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty”.
Kate Phillips, the BBC’s chief content officer, said she hoped the documentary “will resonate with BBC viewers and provide comfort and support to those navigating their own health challenges”.

articles.title: British man recalls ‘despair’ over son’s death after fall from Cyprus window
articles.summary:
Joshua Foster tells of moment he ‘lost control’ of two-year-old when he fell from fourth storey of hotel

A British father who was fined by the courts after his two-year-old son fell from a…

blocks.text: A British father who was fined by the courts after his two-year-old son fell from a fourth-floor window during a family holiday in Cyprus has recalled his “despair” when the boy slipped from his grasp.

Joshua Foster was handed a €3,000 (£2,500) penalty after he pleaded guilty to a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act. Prosecutors in Cyprus had refused to drop the case against him.

During recent court proceedings, it was heard that Foster thought the window at the King Evelthon Beach Hotel & Resort in Chlorakas was closed when he approached it with his son, Jaxon, to show him the view of a waterpark.
The 37-year-old “lost control” of him, the Paphos district court was told, before the boy plunged 10 metres (33ft). The fall happened on 12 July, the first day of the Fosters’ family holiday.

In an interview with the Daily Mail, Foster said: “I have a burden. I’ll have that my whole life. It’s very traumatic. My mind doesn’t want to go there. I just remember the despair of him falling, and watching him fall.
“It was just such a shock … I put him up thinking he was going against a glass pane … and then he wasn’t there.”
The toddler was pronounced dead at Paphos general hospital shortly after he suffered severe cranial injuries when he hit a veranda below.

Foster recalled his outpouring of emotion when he located his son after the fall. “I picked him up. I held him and screamed,” he said. The Essex-born auditor said he and his wife had an hour with their son’s body after he was pronounced dead.

The decision to charge Foster, reported to be a senior accountant at KPMG, was criticised by his legal representatives, as well as human rights defenders, media pundits and diplomats, arguing that it lacked compassion.

The charge Foster accepted is usually levelled in cases involving fatal traffic accidents. It carries a maximum penalty of four years in prison, but the fine he was handed was the lightest sentence possible for the offence.
At his sentencing in October, Judge Froso Christodoulidou ruled that Foster would not be jailed, before describing the incident as a “tragic event”.
The court had heard that, while the presence of alcohol had been detected in Foster’s blood, it was not enough to suggest he was impaired to the point where he had “acted recklessly”.
Foster was detained after the fall. He reportedly had to tell his eldest child, a daughter, about her brother’s death via a video call while he was being held.

He posted €30,000 (£26,000) in bail to return to the UK to attend the funeral of his son in August, but was forced, under threat of extradition, to return to Cyprus and surrender his passport by 14 September.

In a push for clemency, Foster’s legal team had appealed in September to the island’s attorney general, Cyprus’s top legal official, to discontinue the criminal procedure on humanitarian grounds. The request was denied.
Since returning home, Foster said the focus of his grieving family had turned to their daughter.
“It’s very difficult,” he said. “She waves at the sky and says: ‘I love you’ to him and blows a kiss. She’s lost her best friend. She’s gone from having a sibling to being an only child.”
