articles.title: Russian strike on Zelenskyy's hometown in central Ukraine kills 2, wounds 60
articles.summary: A Russian strike on the centre of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown, Kryvyi Rih, killed two people and wounded 60 others, local officials said Saturday.

image.caption: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at a news briefing in Copenhagen, Denmark, on Nov. 10. (Emil Helms/Ritzau Scanpix/Reuters)

blocks.text: A Russian strike on the centre of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown, Kryvyi Rih, killed two people and wounded 60 others, local officials said Saturday.

A seven-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman were killed in the attack Friday night on the city in central Ukraine, the head of the city administration, Oleksandr Vilkul, wrote on the Telegram messaging service.
Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the regional military administration, said 60 people were wounded, including six children.
The strike caused four fires and damaged about 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools and an industrial facility, as well as businesses and vehicles, Vilkul said.
The attack fits the pattern of Moscow's heavy responses to eye-catching Ukrainian attacks, such as the ones this week on the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to illegally annexed Crimea.
The site of a Russian drone and missile attack on Friday night in central Kryvyi Rih, Zelenskyy's hometown. (Press service of the National Police of Ukraine/Reuters)

The missile attack came hours after two Russian missiles and a suspected drone came down in Poland, in what its prime minister said was likely a provocation timed to coincide with European military exercises in his country for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine.
European troops were taking part on Friday in an unprecedented two-week military exercise that began Nov. 9 in southeastern Poland.

items: Trump greets 'my friend' Putin at China summit

blocks.text: Forces are preparing for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine aimed at helping to stabilize the country and rebuild its military.
European countries previously have expressed alarm at what they deem to be Russia's attempts to destabilize the continent.
The aftermath of Friday night's Russian drone and missile attack in central Kryvyi Rih. The attack killed two people, including a child. (Press service of the National Police of Ukraine/Reuters)
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said in Warsaw on Saturday that the alliance is commited to defending "every inch of ​Polish territory."
The development stoked tensions between Europe and Moscow as the U.S. tried to build momentum for talks on ending the war, which began with Russia's invasion on Feb. 24, 2022.

U.S. President Donald Trump discussed the war with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a summit in China on Thursday, according to his envoy, Steve Witkoff. Trump called Putin his "friend" during the meeting and continued to tout their relationship at a White House news conference on Friday.

David McGuinty, Canada's defence minister, said in an interview with CBC's Adrienne Arsenault that Ottawa and leaders in Europe are anticipating the Trump administration will become "less forthcoming" in its support for Ukraine, but noted Canada is staying the course.
"The United States is going to do what the United States is going to do as a sovereign country," McGuinty said.
"But we're … working hand-in-glove with our European colleagues to make sure that the Ukrainians get the support they need."
Zelenskyy calls Putin 'a killer'
Asked about Trump's remarks in an interview with CNN, Zelenskyy called Putin "a killer."
"For us, he is an enemy. And of course, for us, he is a killer," Zelenskyy said Friday. He warned that describing the Russian leader in friendly terms could mean "he doesn't feel enough pressure."
Trump, Xi and Putin release 'peace declaration' with no mention of Ukraine or Iran

Elsewhere in Ukraine, 11 people, including two children, were wounded when a Russian drone attacked a five-storey apartment building in the Kharkiv region, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said Saturday. One person was wounded in a Russian attack on the capital, Kyiv, according to the service.
In Russia, local officials said Saturday that Ukrainian drone attacks wounded three people in the Bryansk and Belgorod border regions.
A firefighter works at the site of a Russian missile strike in Kyiv, during Russia's attack on Ukraine on Friday night into Saturday. (Press service of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine/Reuters)
Russian cargo vessel on fire in Finnish waters
Meanwhile, Russian officials said on Saturday that a cargo vessel bound for Kaliningrad was attacked by two drones in neutral waters.
The crew was being evacuated and the extent of the damage was being assessed, said Aleksandr Drozdenko, the Leningrad regional governor, shortly after the attack was first reported.

The ship caught fire after being hit by drones in the Baltic Sea and later drifted into Finnish waters, prompting Helsinki to impose temporary air and maritime restrictions. It said Ukraine was probably behind the attack.
The Russian cargo ship Sparta II is seen damaged in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday. (Finnish Border Guard/Reuters)
Finland's Border Guard said there was no danger to people or maritime traffic, that rescue units were at the scene, and that it was co-ordinating operations with neighbouring countries.
The Sparta II vessel is known to have links to Russia's armed forces, Finnish Border Guard Cmdr. Ilja Iljin told Reuters.
"At the moment, there is no confirmed information about what cargo is on board, but it cannot be ruled out that there is military material on board," he said.

items: Russia fires hundreds of missiles, drones at Ukraine — and allegedly into Poland

blocks.text: "The war is spilling over into our neighbouring areas. Finnish authorities are handling the situation in the Gulf of Finland, where a drone strike has hit a Russian merchant vessel. Ukraine has the right to fight against the aggressor," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said on X.
Ukraine's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Russia's embassy in Helsinki did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The vessel is subject to U.S. sanctions and is linked to Russian shipping company Oboronlogistika, according to the U.S. Treasury Department.
Oboronlogistika provides logistics services for the Russian defence ministry, according to the company's website.

Kaliningrad Gov. Alexei Besprozvannykh said the incident posed no threat to supplies to the region. Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea that borders Poland and Lithuania, has occasionally been a flashpoint between Russia, the European Union and NATO.

articles.title: Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
articles.summary: Fausto Isidro "Chapo Idisro" Meza Flores, who is accused of drug trafficking and torture, is detained after gun fight with authorities.

blocks.text: A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.
Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained along with his lieutenant by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.

Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.
Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.

Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.

Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores and his second-in-command, it added.
Videos circulating online appear to show helicopters firing streams of bullets towards the ground in Guasave. Others appear to show people at a baseball stadium fleeing as they hear shooting sounds.
The two detainees were subsequently flown to Mexico City to face prosecution, the defence secretariat said.
When he was added to the FBI's most-wanted list in 2025, he was accused of "heinous crimes" including kidnapping, extortion and torture.
Then-acting FBI director Brian Driscoll said Meza Flores and his organisation had also unleashed a "scourge of illicit drugs" into the US via its southern border with Mexico.
He was initially charged with drug trafficking in the US in 2012 before being charged again in 2019.
The 44-year-old is alleged to have conspired to manufacture and distribute large quantities of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana between 2005 and 2019.
Meza Flores was originally a high-ranking member of the Beltrán Leyva Organization, but a split between rival factions led to a surge of violence and prompted him to establish his own cartel by 2013.

His organisation has also engaged in what US officials described as an "extremely violent turf war" with the Sinaloa Cartel, one of the most powerful drug trafficking gangs, which operates in the same region.
Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list after Mexican authorities reportedly linked his cartel to 20 million fentanyl pills they seized in 2024.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has taken a tougher stance on the country's cartels in a bid to resist US intervention on Mexican soil. Mexico has welcomed closer collaboration but resisted US boots on the ground.
Trump made stemming the flow of drugs into the US across its southern border one of his key election pledges.

articles.title: A real '3 Body Problem': Astronomers discover a nearby 'weirdo' triple-star system
articles.summary: An international team of astronomers led by the University of Montreal has found a nearby triple-star system, much like the one in the Netflix show 3 Body Problem. But this one seems to be… a little…

image.caption: An artistic illustration shows the Welopō'ai triple-star system, located just 28 light-years from Earth. The system consists of a red dwarf star, right, and a closely orbiting white dwarf, left, with a second white dwarf, upper, orbiting the pair at a much greater distance. (Benoît Gougeon/Universit

blocks.text: Roughly 28 light-years from Earth lies a peculiar star system called IRAS 21500+5903.

For years, astronomers had known about the two stars that orbited one another. But then, when looking for exoplanets — planets that orbit other stars — a group of astronomers made a surprising discovery: there was another star in the system. Instead of being a binary star system, this was a triple-star system.

"It's a freak thing. It was an annoying object," said Étienne Artigau, a researcher at the Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets (IREx) at the University of Montreal. "It's not what we were looking for."
Their findings were released this week in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

The system contains a red dwarf, a type of star that is very common in our galaxy, and two smaller, dense white dwarfs. One is roughly 1,000 astronomical units (the distance between the sun and Earth) away from the red dwarf. The other, they found, was a mere two astronomical units away, a little similar to the distance from the sun to Mars.
The inner white dwarf orbits the red dwarf, while the outer white dwarf orbits the pair.
A quirky neighbour
What's surprising is that no one had discovered it over the decades.

"It's weird that no one found the system, but it also says that there are weird things overlooked just next to us," Artigau said. "It's like not next door, but down the road, just one block away of a stellar neighbourhood."

When a low- to medium-mass star reaches the end of its life, it first swells into a red giant before leaving behind the dense and small white dwarf. It is what will happen to our own sun in roughly five billion years.
This artist concept depicts an ultra-dense dead star, called a white dwarf, passing in front of a small red star. (NASA/JPL-Caltech)

While looking for an exoplanet in this system, the international team of astronomers — led by the University of Montreal team — used an instrument at the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope in Maunakea, Hawaii, called SPectropolarimètre InfraROUge (SPIRou). It is used to detect exoplanets and does this by measuring tiny changes in a star's velocity, which can be caused by orbiting planets.
But the red dwarf wasn't doing what it was supposed to be doing. It was moving differently, with velocity changes of nearly 16 kilometres a second. That's a huge difference.
Initially, they thought it was a brown dwarf, a type of substellar object that has a mass of about 75 times that of Jupiter.
But that still didn't make sense.
More weirdness
The velocities were so off that they broke Artigau's code.

"At some point, we said, Okay, we should get to the end of it. Something's wrong with that object. And so I fixed the code," he said. "And then we just said, let me do the math of that brown dwarf. Okay, no, it doesn't work."
It was a real head-scratcher.

items: Are we alone? Institute searching for alien signals is using a new way to answer that age-old question
Astronomers think they've captured a planet forming around a host star — something never seen before

blocks.text: What they eventually discovered is that what was causing the perturbations was a high-mass… something. But it also couldn't be seen.
Could it be a black hole? A neutron star? A white dwarf?

The team turned to the Gemini North telescope, also on Maunakea. Using high-resolution images from its 'Alopeke instrument — a specialized high-speed camera — they found what they were looking for: a faint companion star — a white dwarf — orbiting closely around the red dwarf.
Here's where it gets weirder.

Before becoming a white dwarf, the star would have become a red giant. As it swelled up, its orbit would have been so close to the red dwarf that the pair must have interacted with one another. Many times these types of stars envelop the red dwarf, or the two may even merge. This didn't happen.
And there was more.
The inner white dwarf should be spiralling inward toward the red dwarf. Instead, it is in a stable orbit.
It could be that the more distant white dwarf is somehow stabilizing the orbit, though they don't know yet how. That's for future research.

The image on the left shows the two components of the system: Welopō'ai A, a closely orbiting red dwarf and white dwarf pair, and Welopō'ai B, a second white dwarf located farther away. The image on the right provides a close-up view of the inner pair and their orbital paths. (Pan-STARRS1/STScI/MAST, left, International Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab, right. Graphical construction by Étienne Artigau & Heidi White (UdeM/IREx))
"We're saying it cannot exist," Artigau said. "Of course, it exists. It's there."
Paul Delaney, professor emeritus of physics and astronomy at York University in Toronto, believes that perhaps the more distant white dwarf was once much closer to the other pair.

"I mean, when planetary systems form now, one of the standard things is migration," he said. "I would bet that they were relatively proximate to each other and then they did engage in a bit of gravitational embracing, and the further white dwarf today was much, much closer in its heyday."

To add to the weirdness, the astronomers calculated that the system is roughly 10 billion years old, older than our own solar system of 4.6 billion years, and its stars are metal-rich. Typically, these older stars are metal-poor.
"It's tantalizing, and we just don't know if it means anything. It may just be a random draw basically of a stellar population," Artigau said.
Still searching for an exoplanet

The astronomers gave this system the Hawaiian name Welopō'ai, combining "welo" which means an inherited family trait, and "pō'ai," which means an orbit or circular path. The name therefore means "path of family traits."
The very popular book and Netflix show 3 Body Problem looks at a triple-star system and the effects it could have on a nearby planet, mainly to a civilization that has evolved on that planet.
One of the terms that is used to describe the triple-star system in the show is "chaotic," which affects the speed at which the civilization can evolve.

The issue is an age-old physics problem. Two-body systems are predictable. But add a third, and everything blows up. That's because Body A pulls on Body B and Body C. Body C in turn pulls on Body A and Body B, and because of these interactions, it changes their motions and their forces forever.
While researchers didn't find an exoplanet, Artigau said the search isn't over.
"It's such a weirdo system that Atanas Stefanov, one of the authors, he's applying for time to get, to look for planets around the red dwarf," he said.
Whether there is a planet there or whether an alien civilization could live on a planet in a triple-star system remains to be seen.
For Artigau, he said the fact that something new was thrown at him was very exciting.
"I like it," he said. "Little things that are just sideways in your life in research. It's fun."

articles.title: Denmark to expel Russian diplomat over alleged Moscow link to attempted killing of rapper
articles.summary:
Russian intelligence thought to be behind plan to kill US-Ukrainian musician Kyivstoner before concert in Denmark

Denmark’s foreign minister has said Russia’s defence attache in Copenhagen…

blocks.text: Denmark’s foreign minister has said Russia’s defence attache in Copenhagen would be expelled after Moscow was suspected of being behind an attempted killing of a US-Ukrainian rapper.

“We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the ministry of foreign affairs and notified him of the government’s decision to expel the Russian defence attache from Denmark,” Lars Løkke Rasmussen told a news conference. The expulsion will happen within seven days.
“We are saying this very clearly: we have exposed you,” he added.
Danish police said they had averted an attempt by Russian intelligence services ⁠to kill the US-Ukrainian rapper Kyivstoner in September before a planned performance in Denmark.

Rasmussen also said that Denmark was considering suspending Schengen visas to Russians. “We have launched work at the European level to further tighten the rules governing access of Russian nationals to Europe,” he said. “We are now stepping up our efforts towards a halt to all non-essential visas.
“The strongest response Denmark can give is not to waver and to support Ukraine. And we fully intend to continue supporting Ukraine.”

According to Reuters, Rasmussen sent a message on Friday evening to senior European diplomats ‌proposing that the EU should halt tourist visas for Russian citizens and cease recognition of Russian non-biometric passports throughout the 29-nation Schengen free-travel zone.

“We must take concrete actions that project European strength ‌and decisiveness,” the message said. “There is clear momentum to act decisively now, and we should seize this moment to replace our current patchwork ​of national measures with a truly unified EU-wide approach.”

The note also urged each EU member state to offer Russians more limited visas that do not allow travel to other countries in the Schengen zone, and to set tougher entry restrictions for serving and former Russian soldiers.

Police ⁠thwarted the alleged ⁠plot when ​they arrested three men with links to the Danish criminal underworld shortly before Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Viktorovich Vasiliev, was due to perform at a ⁠concert on 25 September, which was then cancelled, officials said. Vasiliev holds US and Ukrainian nationality.

Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen, the head of Denmark’s national security and intelligence service, said: “It is our clear assessment that the assassination attempt was planned by the Russian ⁠intelligence services.”

According to prosecutors, the suspects were driving towards the concert venue north of Copenhagen with two loaded pistols and two knives when police arrested them at about 9.55pm, five minutes before the concert was due ‌to begin. A fourth suspect was arrested later that evening, police said.
One of the suspects had bought a ticket to the concert, according ​to the charges.

The suspects are charged under Section 108 of Denmark’s criminal code, which covers assisting a foreign intelligence service, as well as attempted murder. They denied wrongdoing in court, the broadcaster DR reported.
Kieffer-Kristensen said: “A Russian assassination attempt is not something we’ve seen in Denmark before, ⁠and that gives me an impression of an increasingly aggressive and ​risk-taking Russia.
“We believe ​that the case is important ​for understanding the threat that Denmark faces from Russia.”

The European Commission president, Ursula ​von der Leyen, said the EU ​stood in full solidarity with Denmark and with all member states targeted ​by Russian hybrid ‌attacks. She said the ​bloc would soon ​propose a “new European security strategy” to reinforce preparedness and deterrence.
The Russian embassy ⁠in Copenhagen said that Denmark’s accusations were not backed with ​proof.

articles.title: Cold gives way to rain in parts of UK as weather warning issued for south-west England
articles.summary:
Flood alerts in place and risk of power cuts as more than 100mm predicted to fall on Dartmoor on Sunday

Cold snaps are to make way for heavy rain in some parts of the country as the Met…

blocks.text: Cold snaps are to make way for heavy rain in some parts of the country as the Met Office issued a weather warning for south-west England.
It said there will be a slow-moving band of rain moving across Devon and Cornwall, with more than 100mm due to fall on Dartmoor.
The warning will be in place from 6am on Sunday until midnight.
The Met Office said there was a risk of power cuts and added that driving conditions could be difficult. There are active flood alerts in the area.
It comes as cold weather health warnings are in place in northern England until Tuesday morning. Friday night saw the lowest temperature this autumn.
North-west and north-east England, and Yorkshire and the Humber, have had yellow alerts issued by the UK Health Security Agency.
It suggests there is a risk to vulnerable people, the conditions may put pressure on the health service and people should take care when travelling.

Friday night had the lowest temperature since early January, as Tulloch Bridge in the Scottish Highlands recorded -10.6C. It beat this autumn’s record of -8.4C at the same weather station on Thursday.
The Met Office said there could be a widespread frost across the UK on Saturday night, but there will be warmer and largely drier conditions outside south-west England on Sunday.
The Met Office chief forecaster, Matthew Lehnert, said: “Within the warning area, 20-40mm of rain is likely quite widely, but some parts of south Devon and Cornwall could see 60-80mm.
after newsletter promotion
“Over Dartmoor, there is a chance of more than 100mm falling through the day.

“This slow-moving band of rain will gradually ease on Sunday night, but flooding and travel disruption is possible within the warning area, with south Devon and south Cornwall more likely to see higher totals.
“There is still some uncertainty about where the heaviest rain will fall, so it’s important to stay up to date with the forecast and any warning updates.”

articles.title: Germany's religious freedom report: Authoritarian regimes, holy wars, and spies abroad
articles.summary: Harassment, persecution, surveillance: Across much of the world, people of faith are facing growing pressure. A new German government report is unusually direct in criticizing China in particular.

image.caption: Not all faithful around the globe are free to practice their religionImage: Stanislav Varivoda/ITAR-TASS/IMAGO

blocks.text: The report spans more than 150 pages, but its conclusion can be summed up in a single sentence: "The global situation regarding freedom of religion and belief deteriorated during the reporting period," said Thomas Rachel, the German government's commissioner for freedom of religion and belief, and a member of parliament for the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU). Recently adopted by the Cabinet, the government's fourth report on the subject covers developments from 2023 to 2025.

The government has issued a dedicated report on freedom of religion and belief around the world. According to the report, this freedom is facing "increasing pressure" globally. The focus is not primarily on the suppression of religious institutions or structures, but on the situation of individuals who hold a religious belief, or none at all.
Faith in the Digital Age
Authoritarian regimes increase pressure on religious communities

The importance of religious freedom is reflected in the way the government commissioner describes the issue: "Religion and faith are of great importance to four out of five people around the world and are central to their identity. People wake up with God and go to sleep with God. It is part of their everyday lives." Research by the Pew Research Center suggests that about 84% of the world's population identifies with a certain religion.

At a time when authoritarian regimes are gaining ground and expanding their surveillance capabilities, the report paints a bleak picture. The growing number of violent conflicts, the rise of authoritarian rule, and the spread of populism have led to "painful restrictions on freedom of religion and belief around the world."

The German government report does not attempt to provide a statistical tally of attacks or the number of people facing persecution. Instead, it examines 30 countries as case studies where, in the federal government's view, freedom of religion and belief is being restricted. These include about six countries each from Africa, Asia, and the Arab world. In Europe, the report focuses on Belarus, Russia, Ukraine, and Turkey, while in Latin America it highlights Mexico, Nicaragua, and Cuba. It also identifies shortcomings in five of the world's six most populous countries: China, India, Indonesia, Pakistan, and Nigeria.
India: Hindu nationalists force religious conversions

Regarding India, the report refers to "Hindu nationalist efforts" that threaten the equal treatment of all officially recognized religions. It states that the generally peaceful coexistence of different faiths is "repeatedly overshadowed by tensions and, at times, violence." Both Muslim and Christian communities report growing intolerance and hate speech. According to the report, violent Hindu extremist groups have carried out a "large number of physical attacks" against Muslims, while the police and government authorities often respond inadequately.

In China, the German government identifies a "significant tightening of the legal framework of state control at the expense of freedom of religion and belief." According to the report, this particularly affects Uyghurs, Tibetans, and churches that lack official state approval and are subject to harsh measures by the authorities. The law on the "Promotion of Ethnic Unity and Progress," which came into force on July 1, 2026, subordinates religion to "the formation of national identity" and patriotic education.

One of the countries where the situation has deteriorated most dramatically is Nicaragua, which has severely restricted freedom of religion and belief since 2018. The repression has primarily targeted the Catholic Church. According to the report, "intimidation, persecution, imprisonment, and expulsion" have forced around 130 priests and nuns to leave the country.
Exploring Africa's indigenous religions

The reports reserves some of its sharpest criticism for Kirill, the patriarch of the Russian Orthodox Church. Under his leadership, the church has strongly supported Russia's war against Ukraine and portrayed it as a "holy war." According to the report, "weapons are blessed, Russian soldiers are absolved of their sins, and donations are collected for the war." It is perhaps the clearest example in the report of how religion can be used to justify oppression and violence.
Intimidation reaches beyond borders

The report explicitly addresses the threat posed by "transnational repression" (TNR), which it describes as a "growing global problem" that also affects Germany. The term refers to the persecution or intimidation of individuals by their country of origin beyond its own borders.

Ultimately, it argues, this amounts to a "continuation of domestic repression." Such "cross-border repression" has become considerably easier through the growing availability of digital means of repression, including smear campaigns on social media and spyware.

These forms of pressure range from physical attacks on individuals to digital assaults such as online intimidation and defamation. In some cases, repression is also carried out by threatening family members who remain in the country of origin. Russia and Iran, for example, are identified as the "main perpetrators of transnational repression" in Germany.

China is a particularly prominent example of religious and ideological tensions. Repression by Beijing in Germany primarily targets members of groups that the country's Communist Party classifies as "hostile to the system." These include Uyghurs, Tibetans, and members of the Falun Gong movement. According to the report, they are "also subject to surveillance and repressive measures in Germany," while relatives living in China are pressured.

Thomas Rachel hopes the newly published report will be "discussed in as many Bundestag committees as possible" and that members of parliament will "engage with the issue accordingly." Previous government reports on the subject have been debated in the Bundestag plenary at least once and, in some cases, twice.
Sweden: Hybrid warfare in a Russian Orthodox church
Religion: A matter of German foreign policy

The issue's place within the German government has also changed during the current legislative term. Commissioner Thomas Rachel is now based at the Foreign Ministry, while both of his predecessors since 2018 were attached to the Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development. Today, Rachel says, the importance of religion is being "taken into account" in German foreign policy. He also points to his involvement in the Foreign Ministry's diplomatic training programs.

In doing so, the government led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) reversed a structural decision made by the previous center-left coalition, which was led from 2021 to 2025 by Chancellor Olaf Scholz of the Social Democratic Party (SPD). The Scholz government had reduced the issue's prominence by assigning it to the "Religion and Foreign Policy" division. Religion and foreign policy have now regained a more prominent place within government.

One example is the current foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, who has already visited the Vatican more often than his two predecessors combined. In addition, alongside Rachel, the ministry has for some time maintained a dedicated unit headed by an ambassador that deals with, among other things, "fundamental issues relating to religion and foreign policy."

articles.title: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
articles.summary: Ukraine's president says Kyiv acted after 109 separate Russian aerial attacks on bridges in Ukraine.

blocks.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.

In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".
He also rejected the claim the Russian president made in China that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsular it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.
"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.
The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.
"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."
The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.
"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.
He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".
The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".
Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".
Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders met in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys to discuss Ukraine.
That meeting came hours after Putin held trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.
"I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate."

Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."

articles.title: 'We are sorry': Rocks found in restaurant burritos in Alberta
articles.summary: BarBurrito issued an apology to its customers after pea-sized stones were found in some of its burritos at restaurants in Alberta. The company says the rocks came from a particular brand of beans…

image.caption: A small rock found inside a burrito purchased Nov. 2 from BarBurrito in southeast Calgary. The company has apologized for rocks found in its food, saying they've linked them to a particular brand of beans from its food supplier. (Saskia McNeill)

blocks.text: Calgary

BarBurrito issued an apology to its customers after pea-sized stones were found in some of its burritos at restaurants in Alberta. The company says the rocks came from a particular brand of beans that it is no longer using.
BarBurrito switching bean supplier after at least 3 incidents where small rocks found in food

A Calgary woman who found a pea-sized rock in her burrito is pleased to see an apology from the company, but questions why it took BarBurrito 17 days to respond to her complaints and issue a public notice.
Saskia McNeill, her husband and their six-year-old son ordered home delivery Nov. 2 from BarBurrito, a Canadian restaurant chain with hundreds of locations across the country.
After five or six bites into her burrito, she chomped down on something that didn't feel right.
“I just felt something like, very hard. And then I just took it out and discovered it was a stone basically the size of a pea,” McNeil said from her home in southeast Calgary.
She doesn't think any of her teeth were damaged, but she quickly put an end to dinner time. She told her family to stop eating and then called the restaurant multiple times without getting through.
Saskia McNeill retrieves a small rock she found inside a burrito purchased from BarBurrito in Calgary. (Bryan Labby/CBC)
The family then drove to the strip mall in the community of Legacy where the restaurant is located, and spoke to an employee she described as sympathetic.
"He took a picture of the stone. He was very friendly. He was very understanding and he took our number and he reassured that the manager was going to give us a call."
She says that didn't happen.
A week later, with frustration mounting, McNeill posted an online review of the restaurant and was stunned to see someone else had found a rock in their burrito.
A review posted by someone who found a rock inside their burrito purchased at BarBurrito in southeast Calgary. (Google Reviews)
McNeill says it was upsetting to see the second stone show up after she warned the restaurant about her discovery.
“All I wanted was this location to take safety seriously," she said.
A third rock was found inside a burrito purchased at BarBurrito in Canmore, Alta.
The partner of a CBC journalist said he found this rock in a burrito he bought in Canmore in September.
A small stone found in a burrito purchased at BarBurrito in Canmore, Alta. (Submitted by Aaron Wright)
McNeill says after she saw the second stone review she contacted Alberta Health Services' environmental public health branch to report the incident.
She shared her experience and photos with a food inspector, who visited and inspected the restaurant, according to AHS.

AHS said in an email that "to date EPH has received one complaint of this nature." It provided no other information related to the investigation, but did say it takes all complaints seriously and follows up on concerns brought to its attention.
Manager, company apologize
McNeill says the inspector told her he visited the restaurant this week and on Wednesday the store manager contacted her.
“She was very respectful. She apologized so many times."
CBC News reached out to the company on Thursday and within hours it posted a message on its website apologizing for the unwanted ingredients in its food.
"Some of our guests have found small stones in beans served at our restaurants in Calgary and Canmore. We are sorry. That should never happen in food we serve."
The company says other locations in Western Canada may have been affected as well.
In an email to the CBC, the company said the "source of the rocks" has been linked to a particular brand of beans the company purchases from a food distributor in Western Canada.
A notice to customers inside the BarBurrito in southeast Calgary on Nov. 19, 2026. (Bryan Labby/CBC)

"As a result, we have removed all beans from this supplier across all affected locations. We’re actively procuring beans from alternative suppliers which currently supply our Eastern Canada locations."
It says all locations remain open and once the bean supply has been restored, the company says it will add extra inspections before the beans are prepared.
McNeill says she doesn't understand why the company took so long to respond to her complaints and suggests inquiries from CBC News may have expedited the response.
“It was just the non-communication, the not responding, that's what I don't understand.”
She says she turned down refund and gift card offers from the company.
"It's not about getting a free meal. It's about the safety. And all we wanted from you guys is to let us know you're taking care of that."

articles.title: Haitians excited but uneasy as El Salvador troops fight gangs
articles.summary:
Foreign combatants in Port-au-Prince welcomed by many after years of gang control but some fear offensive could exacerbate volatile situation

A bullet-peppered mural of the Haitian striker…
articles.byline: Etienne Côté-Paluck in Port-au-Prince and Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: A bullet-peppered mural of the Haitian striker Emmanuel Sanon covers the facade of Port-au-Prince’s main football ground. But more than two years have passed since any sports stars graced the pitch.

In 2024, as the surrounding city was almost entirely captured by heavily armed gangs, Sylvio Cator stadium – where football greats including Brazil’s Ronaldo and Roberto Carlos once played – also fell under criminal control, its dilapidated red and blue stands used as an outpost by fighters working for a gang boss called Izo. Haiti’s national team, the Grenadiers, found itself homeless and was forced to play its World Cup qualifying games abroad.

That changed last week, as Haitian police and troops from El Salvador reconquered the stadium. Nayib Bukele, El Salvador’s authoritarian president, called the development a step towards delivering Haiti from a criminal insurrection that has displaced more than 1.5 million people and killed thousands.
“We now have the upper hand on the ground,” claimed Bukele, who has sent more than 2,000 soldiers to Haiti since mid-October.

blocks.caption: Salvadoran troops near the mural of the Emmanuel Sanon. Photograph: Fildor Pq Egeder/Reuters

blocks.text: Outside the Sylvio Cator stadium, named after an acclaimed Haitian athlete who won a silver medal at the 1928 Olympics, there were joyous scenes as citizens celebrated a foreign politician they hope will prove an unlikely saviour.
“There’s a wind of hope blowing through our country and, thanks to God, we will get through this. Long live Bukele!” said a 55-year-old decorator who asked to be named as Bòs Baton.

Stood by Sanon’s battle-scarred fresco, Baton recalled being driven from an area called Poste-Marchand after criminals set his home ablaze during an armed uprising that started in February 2024. “Today, we are happy because there are places we couldn’t go to before that are accessible – and it’s thanks to Bukele’s intervention that we can be here today,” Baton said.

Identical sentiments have been voiced on the streets of El Salvador’s capital, San Salvador, in recent years as a result of Bukele’s controversial anti-gang crusade, which has freed millions from gang rule – albeit at a high price.

Since that crackdown began in early 2022, more than 90,000 Salvadorans have been jailed as part of a mass incarceration campaign that has slashed murder rates but also fuelled fears that El Salvador’s democracy has died.

Bukele’s domestic clampdown has made the millennial strongman a darling for rightwing politicians and voters across Latin America and the Caribbean, who hold his actions up as proof that, with an iron fist and a malleable approach to human rights, rampant criminality can be tamed.
Now, as Bukele seeks to extend his seven-year presidency in an election in February, he is hoping to burnish his gang-busting credentials overseas.

blocks.caption: Nayib Bukele’s crime crackdown in El Salvador has freed millions of people from gang rule – but at a high price. Photograph: Marvin Recinos/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “It’s an operation that projects force, that projects Bukele’s image as the saviour … and positions El Salvador as a key reference in the region for [how] … to deal with gangs and security,” said Tiziano Breda, a Latin America regional expert from the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project.

The extent of Bukele’s ambitions in Haiti is unclear. The operation’s trigger was the 18 October abduction of four Salvadoran aviation technicians who worked for a UN-backed security force. On Monday, Bukele’s vice-president, Félix Ulloa, announced Salvadoran troops would withdraw as soon as the four men were rescued, “because this is not an occupying force – we are not there to stay”.
But Ulloa also said his government was responding altruistically “to a cry for help from the Haitian people and government”, suggesting its mission could be extended.
Bukele has also hinted his plans go beyond short-lived ground operations to recover his citizens, or their remains. “We will triumph. God will give us victory,” the politician vowed this week.

Many Haitians hope his combatants will stay and have been thrilled by cinematic social media clips posted by Bukele showing helicopter strikes on a gang compound and the mansion of a gangster nicknamed Taliban.
Banners and billboards around Port-au-Prince celebrate Bukele as a 21st-century liberator and feature slogans such as “The bandits won’t get a wink of sleep!” and “We’re tired! Give us Bukele!”

Standing outside the liberated football ground, bricklayer Venel Saindor recalled how criminals torched his home in Carrefour-Feuilles three years ago. “It’s impossible to enter my neighbourhood because the thieves are still there. They shoot at us,” the 56-year-old explained, lifting his shirt to reveal a bullet scar above his right nipple.
“We need Bukele to help us return to our homes,” added Saindor, as a Salvadoran soldier with a belt-fed heavy machine gun kept watch from the stadium’s terraces.

blocks.caption: Soldiers from El Salvador keep watch from inside the Sylvio Cator stadium. Photograph: Patrice Noel/AP

blocks.text: Monique Clesca, a writer and activist, echoed the bricklayer’s enthusiasm. “Haitians are elated … [and] I feel elated also … It is a moment of hope,” she said on Tuesday, as thousands of demonstrators poured on to the streets to champion Bukele, chanting: “Viv Bukele!” and “Bukele is not playing games!”

As a sea of protesters swept towards the prime minister’s offices, people from all walks of life spoke of how armed groups had destroyed their lives and their collective hope that Bukele may provide a solution.

“I used to drive an old bus. The bandits burned it. They burned my house down too,” said Wilné Persona, a 50-year-old driver, adding: “Bukele is the one we are waiting for … because we can no longer bear the situation.”

blocks.caption: Haitians take to the streets to demonstrate their support for Bukele and his military intervention. Photograph: Patrice Noel/AP

blocks.text: A food vendor called Claudy Mayas urged “Papa Bukele” to stand his ground. “Bukele, I bless you, your wife and your children,” said Mayas, 51. “The Haitian people are with you, just as you are with us.”

Clesca attributed the palpable excitement to the widespread perception that Bukele’s “decisive” action had exposed the incompetence, inefficiency and indifference of Haitian and foreign leaders. “Basically, what Bukele has done is show that leadership is about resolving a problem for your population,” she said, praising how the stadium and other areas were recaptured in less than a month.

Amid the excitement there is also unease. Some fear Bukele’s offensive could exacerbate an already volatile situation in and around Haiti’s capital, much of which resembles a war zone. This week, there was heavy fighting between Salvadoran troops, police and gangs in Village of God, the shantytown that is Izo’s main base. On Thursday, police said officers had killed at least 34 suspected criminals during an operation near the stadium.

Some suspect El Salvador’s president, a social media whiz with 22 million followers on X and TikTok, could be exaggerating his troops’ role in recent successes with help from a strike team of online propagandists and fans. “Nayib Bukele is gang kryptonite,” one US enthusiast gushed this week, calling his intervention “a miracle”.

Others fret over Bukele’s ability to distinguish between gang members and civilians, given the indiscriminate nature of his mass detention campaign in El Salvador, where thousands of innocent people have been jailed without due process.

blocks.caption: Damaged homes and buildings in an area previously controlled by gangs in Port-au-Prince. Photograph: Clarens Siffroy/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Clesca downplayed concerns over the toll Bukele’s crackdown has taken on democracy and the rule of law in El Salvador, which now has the world’s highest per capita incarceration rate. Haitian politics was so contaminated with organised crime, she argued, “it’s almost like the mafia has taken over 10 Downing Street”.
“If you’re talking about [an] assault on democracy, Haiti is … almost a case study that is … even worse, more flagrant, than El Salvador,” Clesca said.

The security situation was so dire that urgent action was needed. “Let’s just be honest … in Haiti, we’re being brutalised,” Clesca said. “Girls are being taken as sexual slaves. They’re being gang raped. So somewhere along the line, we have to say: ‘Haiti helped [South American independence hero] Simón Bolívar [who received shelter and support from Haiti in the early 1800s] … and now, Bukele is helping us’.”

At Tuesday’s rally, protesters spoke of El Salvador’s president in divine terms. “Today, we see Bukele as a saviour, as someone sent by God,” said one man, before adding a word of caution that spoke to countless past interventions that have ended in frustration and failure.
“There is one thing I will say to President Bukele,” he said. “He must not start with us and leave us halfway.”

articles.title: Satellites are constantly photographing Earth. A Waterloo student has compiled the pictures into one spot
articles.summary: Satellites are constantly photographing Earth, and a new website designed by a University of Waterloo student is making these public photos more accessible to the general public.

image.caption: Armaan Gupta is a computer science student at the University of Waterloo. He recently created and launched the website Watched.Earth that shows publicly available satellite photos from anywhere on Earth. (Lauren Kuivenhoven/CBC, (left) Watched.Earth)

blocks.text: Kitchener-Waterloo
Satellites are constantly photographing Earth, and a new website designed by a University of Waterloo student is making these public photos more accessible to the general public.
'That kind of that kind of information should be accessible to everyone,' says Gupta
Satellites are constantly photographing Earth, and a new website designed by a University of Waterloo student is making these photos more accessible to the general public.

Armaan Gupta is a computer science student. As a project one weekend, he decided to make a website, Watched.Earth, when he found out some of his friends were unaware that satellites are perpetually taking pictures of Earth.

When a user clicks on the website they are greeted with an interactive globe. Users can type in an address and will be taken to that place on Earth. The website shows how many satellites passed by over the past seven days, and any publicly available satellite photos. There is also a "surprise me" option, which takes users to a random place on Earth.
A time-lapse feature shows photos from the past 10 years of a specific area. Gupta says the time-lapse feature helps highlight the scale of destruction in war-torn areas.
UW student creates website that shows time-lapse satellite images
Gupta says seeing the progression of destruction in a war-torn area, such as Gaza, Ukraine or South Sudan can be eye-opening for people around the world.

"We always hear about these kinds of things, but it's never really brought to our attention the scale of the destruction. Like, I can't remember the last time it was made like so easily to see exactly how the shape of a particular war zone country has changed throughout the years," Gupta said.
Watched.Earth shows how many satellites passed over an area within the last seven days, along with the recent publicly available photos taken by these satellites. (Watched.Earth)
Although all the photos on Gupta's website are publicly available, he says compiling the photos from websites like NASA and other space agencies into one place makes them more accessible.

"I think that we should make it more accessible to the public that ... like 6,000 satellites are taking images of you every few hours. And so I think that kind of information should be accessible to everyone," said Gupta.
Not for professional analysis

Although the website is helpful for raising awareness about countries experiencing war, or just a spot for a curious person to go, the resolution of the photos are not clear enough for professional analysis, according to one expert.
Nathaniel Raymond is the executive director of the Humanitarian Research Lab at the Yale School of Public Health.
His team investigates war crimes and mass atrocities by analyzing satellite imagery, primarily from Google Earth and other high-resolution data sources.

Raymond says Watched.Earth allows the general public to access low-resolution imagery from one interface and "allows them to interact with it in a general way, but not to the degree you would if you were analyzing it to detect change."
He says when using Watched.Earth, it can be difficult to make out alleyways between buildings or distinguish between structures.
However, the imagery that his team uses has a very high resolution that allows them to tell the difference between models of cars.
"In the case of Sudan, we can see dead bodies on the ground," he said.
Despite the low resolution of most of the images on the website, Raymond says it is useful as an awareness-raising tool for the general public.

"It is important that platforms like this exist to allow members of the public to begin to gain familiarity with what can and cannot be seen at different resolutions, and to begin to understand how in conflict areas, damage happens over time at scale," he said.

A photo of Gaza on the left taken by a satellite Dec. 8, 2015, as shown on Watched.Earth's time-lapse feature. The photo on the right shows the same view of Gaza taken on Nov. 10, 2026. (Watched.Earth)

Gupta says he's received a lot of feedback from users asking for higher resolution photos. He says he's currently in the process of communicating with more satellite organizations to try and gain access to their data.
According to Raymond, higher resolution imagery is often highly access controlled, and isn't updated as regularly as lower resolution satellites.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Lauren Kuivenhoven is a reporter at CBC K-W. She loves hearing from the community and is open to stories at lauren.kuivenhoven@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Woman's airport security ordeal with dad's ashes highlights challenges of travelling with cremated remains
articles.summary: Rules around transporting creamated remains through airports and challenges with new scanners can add "another layer of grief" to an already stressful time, says the head of the Funeral Service…

image.caption: Funeral industry workers have been trying to ensure that travellers know about new screening technology and rule updates concerning transporting cremated remains, says the executive director of the Funeral Service Association of Canada. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Manitoba

Rules around transporting creamated remains through airports and challenges with new scanners can add "another layer of grief" to an already stressful time, says the head of the Funeral Service Association of Canada.
Some urns, containers holding cremated remains being turned away by new scanners at Canadian airports
Niki Trosky said she felt like she was crumbling inside when a red light on a security scanner at Calgary's airport suddenly illuminated as the cremated remains of her late father passed through.

The life coach and author, who is originally from Winnipeg and now has a home in Mexico, was travelling with her father's ashes from Manitoba's capital to Los Angeles, with a brief layover in Calgary, late last month.
"I wanted to bring some of his ashes back here with me so I could have him close," said Trosky, who described her father, Thomas Trosky, as a devoted dad who never let her down.
"[The] best person in the world," she told host Marcy Markusa in an interview with CBC Manitoba's Information Radio earlier this week.
Thomas, a former teacher and decorated sportsman who was affectionately known by the nickname "Trigger," died on July 1.

Niki Trosky says she wanted to bring some of the remains of her late father, Thomas 'Trigger' Trosky, back to her home in Mexico 'so I could have him close,' but she ran into challenges getting them through security screening at the airport in Calgary. (Submitted by Niki Trosky)

While passing through security at Winnipeg's airport with her son, Trosky said staff were compassionate and took her father's cremated remains through a separate screening process. They also told her she would have to go through security again in Calgary before heading to Los Angeles.

With only about an hour between connecting flights, Trosky and her son rushed over to security once they arrived in Calgary. Staff there warned her the airport's new security scanner hadn't been letting some remains through.

"I put him in the bin, and sure enough, he goes through and we get the red light," Trosky said, recounting the worry she felt over whether she'd have to leave her dad behind — or worse, throw him away.
"I can feel this crumbling sensation inside of my body," she said.
Security staff told her to go to the WestJet counter to see if the ashes could be stowed in her checked bags instead. She ran to the desk as fast as she could.
"I had tears in my eyes, and I just said, 'They're not letting me bring my dad on the plane. I need your help,'" Trosky recalled.
The woman behind the counter worked quickly to try to pull the checked bags before they were loaded into the L.A.-bound plane. But it was too late.
Trosky's father's ashes never made it onto that connecting flight.
'Another layer of grief'

Pam Moss, executive director of the Funeral Service Association of Canada, says people may feel a sense of uncertainty when transporting their loved one's cremated remains, adding "another layer of grief to an already very, very difficult time."

That's why funeral industry workers have been trying to ensure that before they jet off to the airport, travellers know about new screening technology and Canadian Air Transport Security Authority rule updates concerning transporting ashes, said Moss.
"We always tell everybody, every funeral director, every family member — go to CATSA's website, because that's what you have to follow," she said.

The air security authority said in a statement to CBC News that passengers are "generally permitted" to take cremated remains with them, but that depends on whether the ashes successfully pass through security screening.

The Canadian Air Transport Security Authority says some urns and containers holding cremated remains haven't been able to pass security screenings since new CT X-ray scanners were installed at some Canadian airports. (Canadian Air Transport Security Authority)

Some urns and containers holding cremated remains haven't been allowed through screenings since CATSA started installing new X-ray security machines that use CT scanning at airports across Canada in 2024, the authority said.

The authority says it is working closely with Transport Canada — which sets the rules — and that it is testing an enhanced screening procedure for urns and other containers at locations across Canada.
Advice for travellers

Cremated remains are a "dense material" that can be hard to screen, CATSA's website says. The ashes must pass screening tests to move on to their next destination, and funeral home documents don't override that requirement, the authority says.

Smaller quantities of 350 millilitres or less — about the size of a regular pop can — are more likely to pass through screening, depending on the container. Plastic, cardboard, cloth and wood are more likely to pass than stone, metal or ceramic, the website says.
Travellers can also ask their funeral director for temporary containers for air transportation, which are more likely to pass screening.

items: Alberta widow calls for policy review after Air Canada temporarily loses husband's ashes

blocks.text: If the container doesn't make it past security, travellers may be able to put it into their checked baggage instead, ship it by mail or cargo, or leave it with someone who isn't travelling.

Moss said having ashes turned away at airport security can be "terribly upsetting," and her group has been raising concerns about the emotional, cultural and religious impact of the recent changes with both CATSA and Transport Canada.
Niki Trosky and her late father. (Submitted by Niki Trosky)
Trosky made the difficult decision to leave her father's ashes behind in Calgary with the WestJet employee behind the desk, Karen D’Costa-Stegemann, who vowed to reunite them.
"She looked at me, and she's, like, 'I'm gonna take care of him. I've got him. I'm going to get your dad to you.' And something in me instantly shifted," Trosky said.
"It's really turned what could have been one of the worst moments of my life into one of the most beautiful."
D'Costa-Stegemann took the remains home with her, placing them temporarily on her own mantle, next to her late husband.
The ashes are now back in Winnipeg with Trosky's mom.
Trosky plans to bring a piece of him from Manitoba to Mexico soon.
"I'll be going home for Christmas, and so hopefully I can bring some of my dad back when I come back from that trip," she said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Lauren Scott is a Winnipeg-based reporter with CBC Manitoba. They hold a master’s degree in computational and data journalism, and have previously worked for the Hamilton Spectator and The Canadian Press.
With files from Emily Enns and Marcy Markusa

articles.title: Judge awards damages to both sides in lawsuit after neighbours' dispute over loose dogs 'spun out of control'
articles.summary: A judge has awarded an eastern Manitoba couple sued by their neighbour $10,000 in damages, and their neighbour $1,000, after an "unfortunate series of events" unfolded over dogs allowed to run loose…

image.caption: A woman's decision to let her rescue dogs roam free on her property led to an 'unfortunate series of events' with her neighbours, a Manitoba judge wrote in a recent decision. (Reshetnikov_art/Shutterstock)

blocks.text: Manitoba

A judge has awarded an eastern Manitoba couple sued by their neighbour $10,000 in damages, and their neighbour $1,000, after an "unfortunate series of events" unfolded over dogs allowed to run loose on an unfenced property.
'Robert Frost knew fences make good neighbours,' Justice Sheldon Lanchbery wrote in decision

The couple — a man and woman, named as the defendants in a lawsuit filed with Manitoba Court of King's Bench — purchased their "dream property" along the Winnipeg River, in the rural municipality of Alexander, in 2015, Justice Sheldon Lanchbery wrote in a Nov. 16 decision.
The property has a large forested area, with walking trails, that shielded them from their neighbours, and offered an escape from the "hustle and bustle of the real world," Lanchbery wrote.
Around 2017, a woman — the plaintiff in the suit — purchased the adjacent property to the east, and decided it would be "a great location" to raise rescue dogs, the decision says.

Though she lacked prior experience in handling rescues, she registered a business as a dog rescue — an idea that "originated during a course of employment on an Indigenous reserve," where dogs roamed freely, Lanchbery wrote.
She decided to also let the dogs she rescued roam on her new property.
"The dogs in question are best described as feral," Lanchbery wrote, and their "aggressive tendencies" continued post-rescue.
Justice Sheldon Lanchbery decided against awarding legal costs to either party, saying in his decision they 'were painfully aware this was not their finest hour.' (Jaison Empson/CBC)
Although the municipality had bylaws in place to restrict the number of dogs a landowner can have on their property, the woman "far exceeded that number," the judge wrote.
"The evidence as to the precise number is inconsistent," but she had at least seven prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, Lanchbery wrote.
The couple said they "did not dare go walking" in the forested area of their property because of the dogs.
The man in the couple testified one of the woman's dogs bit his shin. He also suffered a contusion on one of his hands after he punched the animal, Lanchbery wrote.
'A lot of talking, but not a lot of listening'

The woman had a dog kennel on her property, but the dogs were not always kept there and were not leashed when outside it, the decision says. The woman believed the dogs "should be able to roam," which included defecating on the couple's property.
There were early attempts to resolve the conflict, which Lanchbery described as "a lot of talking, but not a lot of listening."
Accusations "flew back and forth," and "a first-year law student knows what follows next," wrote Lanchbery.
Building a fence between their properties could have solved their problem.Justice Sheldon Lanchbery
Security cameras were installed, and both parties started to photograph and film each other near the property line.
Land surveys were also ordered and boulders were placed near where the dog owner believed the property line was, but another survey done by the couple showed she was incorrect, the decision says.
The woman then approached the couple to ask if they would help pay for a fence to keep her dogs from entering their property.
The couple refused, in part because they felt it was the woman's responsibility to control her dogs, Lanchbery wrote.
He quoted American poet Robert Frost, who "knew fences make good neighbours."
"Building a fence between their properties could have solved their problem," wrote Lanchbery.
Both sides guilty of trespassing
Disputes continued between the parties. The woman purchased a "large, cumbersome" dock, and instead of putting it on her own property, she placed it on the couple's.

"I find if the dock was to be placed in the Winnipeg River, the easiest unimpeded point of access to transport the dock into the Winnipeg River was on the east side of … [the dog owner's] property, not on the west side [closer to the neighbours]," wrote Lanchbery.
The couple put up "no trespassing" signs, " adding to … [the dog owner's] frustration," he wrote.
The woman later accused the couple of trespassing and filed her lawsuit, after the man threw broken boards from the dock into her dog kennel.
One of her dogs suffered an eye injury, but the judge said evidence suggested it likely wasn't from the boards.
The man admitted he had thrown the boards into the kennel, but denied the dog was present when he did so. There was no evidence the dog was in the kennel at the time, Lanchbery wrote.
The judge concluded, however, that both parties were guilty of trespassing — the couple by throwing the deck boards into the kennel, and the woman by letting her dogs run loose.

items: Dispute between neighbours in small Manitoba community ends with 'regrettable' court fight: judge

blocks.text: He awarded the couple $10,000 in aggravated and general damages for the woman's failure to control her dogs, which was ongoing behaviour, compared to the couple's single instance of trespassing, he said.
He also awarded the couple an extra $100 because the woman placed her dock on their property, and parked cars there too, which he said was "an inconvenience at best."

Lanchbery awarded the dog owner $1,000, saying the man's conduct in throwing the boards was "especially egregious" given that he has previous military experience, including training other members in hand-to-hand combat.
The couple's lawyer had argued that given that background, the man had actually "exercised great restraint in not injuring" the woman's dogs, but the judge rejected that argument.
"Removing boards from [her] dock and propelling them into a run are an intentional act of intimidation," he wrote.
The judge decided awarding legal costs to either party was not justified, given their conduct throughout the dispute.
"When the testimony concluded in this action, the litigants were painfully aware this was not their finest hour," he wrote.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Ozten Shebahkeget is a member of Northwest Angle 33 First Nation, born and raised in Winnipeg. She started writing for CBC Manitoba during the first Pathways program in 2022. She holds a master's degree in writing from the University of Saskatchewan.

articles.title: Anthropic researcher uses AI to solve math's greatest riddle
articles.summary: The proposed breakthrough could reshape mathematical research, but still needs independent verification. It's the latest in a string of cases where AI has outpaced humans in solving famous maths…

image.caption: Anthropic's Claude AI tool has done what mathematicians have failed to do for more than a centuryImage: Carlos Barria/REUTERS

blocks.text: A mathematician working for AI giant Anthropic says he used the company's Claude AI tool to solve one of mathematics most famous problems.
The Riemann hypothesis dates back to 1859 and centers on the distribution of prime numbers underpinning a much wider scope of mathematical work.

Levent Alpoge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, made the announcement on his website. "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis," Levent Alpoge wrote in a note released Friday.

The proof still has to be verified and confirmed by other mathematicians. If it withstands independent examination, it would be a major milestone both in mathematics and the growing role of artificial intelligence (AI) in scientific research.
The Riemann hypothesis is the latest and most important in a string of famous mathematical problems that were tackled with the help of AI.
What did Alpoge say about the breakthrough?
Alpoge said that the collaboration with AI had generated more than 250,000 pages of mathematical material, adding that he had not yet mastered all the mathematics involved.

"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," he wrote. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."

blocks.caption: AI is increasingly outpacing humans when it comes to mathematical researchImage: Design Pics/IMAGO

blocks.text: The Riemann Hypothesis is one of seven major mathematical problems, the so-called Millennium Prize Problems, selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which offers $1 million for a solution to each of those.
"This is an announcement of historic significance," Martin Bridson, president of the institute, said in a statement quoted by news agency AP.
He added it "holds the promise of a dramatic transformation in the perception of what is possible in the struggle to extend the human understanding of mathematics."
"But the journey from today’s announcement to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult."
What is the Riemann hypothesis?

Formulated by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in the 19th century, the hypothesis is about the distribution of prime numbers, which are numbers that can only be divided by themselves and the number 1.

The hypothesis describes a fundamental pattern of how these numbers are distributed as they become ever larger. Confirming that hypothesis is thought to have crucial implications for a wide range of further mathematical research.

The potential breakthrough by Alpoge and Claude AI comes amid a growing number of examples where artificial intelligence systems are making significant contributions to advanced mathematical research.
In September, rival AI company OpenAI said its technology had helped solve a problem involving the Navier-Stokes equations.

The equations, which describe the movement of fluids such as water and air, are another of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, but the claim that they've been solved also still needs independent verification.

articles.title: China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve
articles.summary: Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035

blocks.text: China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.

Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”
China is the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases by far, producing more than a quarter of the world’s total, so its push for electrification is significant.

At Cop31, countries are being asked to sign up to a target of deriving 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035. Australia, the president of the negotiations, and the host nation Turkey have pushed the target and on Friday night Australia and China signed a joint statement endorsing the “35:35” goal.

But in the second draft text of the probably outcome from Cop31, released on Thursday, the electrification pledge was downgraded to one of a suite of voluntary options countries can take up to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.

In an interview with the Guardian at the talks, Wang said: “China will do our best to realise clean end-use electrification, and also help other countries to improve. China has significantly reduced the cost of clean technology and products and we would like to share our experience with other countries.”

Experts have said electrification is the next vital step in the shift to a low-carbon economy, as the only way to diminish the close to 80% of fossil fuels still used for primary energy, mostly for transport, heating and industry.

While civil society organisations want any commitment made on electrification to specify that it must be met from clean sources, a pledge that leaves the choice to countries is likely to have more widespread support, as many – including China and India – are resistant to anything they feel smacks of “top down” interference in national plans.

But campaigners argue that allowing individual countries to decide risks leaving the door open to more gas-fired power plants. Some compromise language is also possible that would urge countries to decarbonise their power.

Last year, electricity made up nearly 30% of China’s energy use and it is on track to make that 35% by 2030. Electricity is several times more efficient than fossil fuels, meaning that it takes far less energy to run electric vehicles, heat pumps and industrial processes than their fossil fuel counterparts.

Wang said China was happy with the 2035 target, but that it would be harder to meet if the electricity was required to come entirely from low-carbon sources. “For this target, no problem. But if you think about ensuring clean electrification, that may be a little bit difficult, even for China. For other countries, it’s even more difficult,” he said.
China still has a large number of coal-fired power stations and is planning some new ones, though fewer than before. Wang said this would be used for back-up during the transition to clean energy.

One of the key issues at Cop31 is the “transition away from fossil fuels”, which was one of the resolutions passed at the Cop28 summit in Dubai in 2023, but which countries have failed to flesh out since. The phrase was included in the first draft of the “cover decision” outcome from Cop31, presented on Monday, but excised from the second draftissued on Thursday, to the dismay of many countries and campaigners.
after newsletter promotion

Wang said: “We agree with paragraph 28 of the UAE consensus [the transition resolution]. But maybe different countries have different roadmaps. It’s very difficult to have only one unified roadmap for every country. So maybe we will help other countries to have their own country-based solutions, to realise their own national way of establishing a new renewable-based power system.”

China is also concerned about trade barriers to its clean technology exports, including the tariffs that the US under Donald Trump has placed on Chinese goods, and the “carbon border adjustment mechanism” (CBAM) imposed by the EU. The CBAM penalises imports from countries with looser regulations on carbon than the EU, which forces companies in high-carbon sectors to pay for their carbon emissions in order to level the playing field.

Some smaller developing countries have criticised the EU for its CBAM, warning that it will hamper their manufacturing industries. The EU said it had processes in place to ensure smaller developing countries were not hurt.

Wang called for more work on trade issues at Cops. “They must come together to find a unified approach,” he said. “China and other developing countries, including the global south, disagree [with the EU] on this. But that’s why we should continue to strengthen our dialogue.”

Jiangwen Guo, a senior research fellow at the Chatham House thinktank, said other countries could learn from China. “China has very consistent top-down policies [and] sets a clear direction with high consistency, then follows with learning by doing,” she said. “In the great energy transition, there is no one ahead of China. China is creating the model for the globe.”

Negotiators at Cop31, which was scheduled to end at 6pm on Friday, were sent home late on Friday after the talks stalled, with a new draft text of a “cover decision” marking the main outcome of the negotiations not thought likely to emerge until some time on Saturday morning. The talks are likely to continue into Saturday and potentially beyond.

articles.title: FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
articles.summary: The National Crime Information Center database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information.

blocks.text: The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media report citing two people briefed on the issue.
The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks. The BBC has contacted the FBI for comment.

This comes after string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyberattacks - but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.
White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with US President Donald Trump saying he was not good enough.
It would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US.
In September, the FBI said it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber-crime group ShinyHunters, which claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.

After that hack, one former FBI agent told the BBC he feared for the safety of current employees, whose personal information could soon become available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.
In a separate development, NBC reported an apparent cyberattack against the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) .
Employees were informed on Thursday that its farm payment system had been targeted, NBC said.
The USDA has not publicly commented on the issue.
