Florian Brod, 25, points out: "Almost half of the world's population is under 30, yet only 2.6% of parliamentarians worldwide are under 30."

Young people need and want change to protect their livelihoods and those of future generations. "Yet those who will have to live longest with the consequences of today's decisions are precisely the ones who have hardly any representation in the political decision-making process," says Brod.

At least Brod is somewhat closer to the political decision-making process. He has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two years. In this role, he represents the interests of young people in Germany at United Nations conferences. This is certainly an important step towards giving his generation a greater say in political processes.

blocks.caption: Florian Brod has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two yearsImage: Oliver Pieper/DW

blocks.text: Political participation often remains purely symbolic

Nevertheless, both Florian Brod and Erik Sczygiol, who represents students, have had similar experiences. They often participate in conferences and panel discussions and are invited to submit their opinions, but these invitations often amount to little more than symbolic gestures.

"Having access to an international conference is a first step. But without substantive briefings ahead of the conference, without involvement in preliminary negotiations and, in some cases, without access to negotiation texts, there is little opportunity for us to help shape the outcome. When young people see their demands making little headway politically while they are simultaneously excluded from the search for solutions, frustration inevitably builds," says Brod.

Sczygiol adds: "We often get the feeling at the Federal Youth Conference that we were invited simply to provide a nice photo opportunity. We may be sitting at the table, but often only once a bill has already gone through 17 different drafts and is just days away from its final vote in the Bundestag. By that stage, young people have virtually no say in changing anything, and their voices are barely heard. Their contributions are often simply dismissed with: 'Well, that's just typical youthful nonsense.' And that is something that really frustrates young people."
'Small extremist minority' turn Germany's youth protests violent
The promise that 'our children will have a better life' no longer holds true

Medical student Amélie Belosevic knows that feeling all too well. She served as Germany's Youth Delegate at the World Health Assembly in Geneva this May. Twenty-five countries sent youth representatives, which Belosevic sees as a clear step forward. However, she has one criticism. According to the United Nations Population Fund, 90% of the world's 1.8 billion young people live in the Global South. Yet, the region was represented by only eight delegates. As a result, Africa, Latin America and large parts of Asia were left virtually voiceless.

Her demands for Germany include better job prospects for young people entering the workforce and sustainable pension systems 40 years from now. "For a very long time, people have said, 'I believe my children will have a better life than I do.' But that is no longer necessarily true. So it makes sense then that those who feel the greatest anxiety about the future are the people who have most of their life ahead of them. Sometimes, people don't understand that. We, young people, need to be able to believe in our future again!"

articles.title: Cost of living protests sweep across Europe
articles.summary: Thousands marched across European cities on Friday to protest against the cost of living and other issues.

blocks.text: Protests took place across European cities on Friday as marches were held over the cost of living and other issues, including housing shortages and underfunding in education.
Demonstrations took place in Germany, France, Croatia, Italy, the United Kingdom and elsewhere, attracting a lot of young adults.
The BBC's Europe correspondent, Nick Beake, has been reporting from Rome, where thousands of people took part in a march organised by Italy's main trade union.

articles.title: Anthropic shares fall a day after blockbuster opening
articles.summary: Other tech companies have also taken a hit as share markets broadly slump.

blocks.text: Anthropic's share price has dropped back towards its initial public offering (IPO) price a day after its soaring market debut, as the broader tech sell off continues.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50.
However, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping more than 10% to about $87.30, close to its IPO price of $83, and the broader stock market declines seen on Thursday continued.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index fell 2.8% in morning trade, the S&P 500 was down 1.2% while the Dow Jones Industrial Average remained largely flat.
The maker of the Claude chatbot raised a record $81bn in its initial public offering (IPO), but its share price moved significantly in the first day of trading.
The shares peaked at $115 on Thursday, before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.

Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."

articles.title: What we know about the latest Russian missile strikes on Ukraine
articles.summary: What we know about the latest Russian missile strikes on Ukraine.

blocks.text: Russia targeted bridges in Kyiv and railway stations overnight in a major attack launched days after Ukraine badly damaged the strategically important Crimean Bridge.

Ballistic missiles hit key crossings in the capital during a nationwide assault which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said was "one of the most massive strikes" of the war so far and left at least nine dead.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for the attack on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied peninsula.

The latest Russian strikes coincided with a flurry of talks around the war, and came as the Kremlin pushed back against a US claim that Russia could be open to Western-backed security guarantees for Ukraine.
The BBC's Sarah Rainsford is in Kyiv after the night of strikes.

articles.title: US reacts cautiously to Myanmar genocide ruling as EU praises ‘critical’ role of UN’s top court
articles.summary:
Reactions to ICJ ruling underline global divisions over court with China raising concerns about judicial overreach

The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that

blocks.text: The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, while China has raised concerns of judicial overreach.

Reactions to Thursday’s historic ruling underlined deep international division over the role of the court and similar institutions. The international court of justice (ICJ) had never previously found a state responsible for genocide and the decision could set a precedent for future genocide claims, notably a case against Israel.

The EU hailed a “landmark” judgment from the ICJ, while the UK reaffirmed “full support” for the court and the international legal order. Australia called on Myanmar to comply fully with the judgment and its obligations under international law.

But China, which has offered rare international support for Myanmar’s military rulers since they seized power five years ago, highlighted “issues such as jurisdiction overreach and expanded interpretation”.

“China … believes that such practices are not conducive to the settlement of disputes,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told a news briefing when asked about the ICJ ruling. “The international community should make joint efforts in this direction to avoid complicating this issue.”
Western nations cut ties with the unstable and poor south-east Asian country after the 2021 coup that ousted a civilian-led government.

Myanmar’s presidential spokesperson said on Friday that the ruling was “unfair”, noting the judges’ nine to six vote. The country’s military rulers have denied carrying out a genocide, claiming their actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted insurgent attacks.

“When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” said Khaing Khaing Soe, speaking at a press conference in the capital, Naypyidaw. “So this was not a unanimous decision … I would say it is not fair.”
The US state department said on Thursday that Washington was examining the judgment, while stressing the need to avoid “politicisation” of the ICJ.
Donald Trump’s administration has taken a dim view of international law, vowing to dismantle the international criminal court (ICC), but has yet to question the legitimacy of the ICJ.

The state department reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”, noting that the US was the largest single humanitarian donor to the Rohingya humanitarian crisis response.
In Brussels, the EU said Myanmar must fully implement the ICJ’s ruling “without delay” and that “compliance with ICJ’s decisions is not optional, it is an obligation under international law”.

“The European Union holds the ICJ in the highest regard and remains steadfast in its support for its critical role in the peaceful resolution of disputes and the upholding of the rule of law at international level,” an EU spokesperson said in a statement.

blocks.caption: Rohingya refugees attend a rally addressed by the UN general assembly president, Khalilur Rahman, in Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh on Friday. Photograph: Mohammad Ponir Hossain/Reuters

blocks.text: “The Rohingya people have endured immense suffering, including displacement and violence, and their plight must not be forgotten. This landmark ruling underscores the imperative of justice for victims and the necessity of upholding international law.”
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, called the ruling “a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand”.
The UK expelled Myanmar’s defence attache and called for measures to “ensure the court’s ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity”.

The ruling caps a lengthy legal campaign since August 2017 when Myanmar’s military launched what it called a “clearance campaign” in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. Reports rapidly emerged of mass rapes and killings by security forces, as well as the burning of thousands of homes.

Judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.

The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the ICC – which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states – on allegations of crimes against humanity.

The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited.
While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.
Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part”.

About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across the Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.

blocks.caption: An aerial view shows the Rohingya refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. Photograph: Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: Judges at the court based in The Hague have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.

South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion. An interim ICJ judgment in 2024 ordered Israel to ensure its forces do not commit acts of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia. Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

articles.title: ‘Traumatizing’: hunger striker in ICE detention tells of force-feeding ordeal – and what made him crack
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Luis Alejandro Cora Perez says in messages to Guardian from inside Texas facility pain of force-feeding caused him to break strike

The text message that came from inside the…

blocks.text: The text message that came from inside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center was stark: “I have spent five days eating regular food. If I don’t eat it, they put the tube in me to feed me.”

A Cuban asylum seeker, Luis Alejandro Cora Perez, 32, said in messages to the Guardian this month that he was still weak and dizzy after three months without eating, but that he had broken his hunger strike because being force-fed was just too painful.
The Trump administration responded to requests for comment by denying it had force-fed Cora Perez. But the detainee sent more details – and his is far from an isolated case.
Cora Perez was one of two men on hunger striker at a Texas facility for whom ICE sought and received a federal judge’s permission to force-feed in recent weeks, a Guardian investigation found.

Cora Perez and the other man were locked up inside the Port Isabel service processing center, an ICE detention facility in south Texas, just a few miles from the US-Mexico border, on the coast near where Elon Musk’s SpaceX launches rockets. Cora Perez began a hunger strike in August to protest against his prolonged detention by federal immigration officials while his case plays out. At first he only drank water, then after three weeks, he says he began to drink one Ensure nutritional shake per day.
On 30 October, court records show ICE received permission to forcibly feed and hydrate him, and to restrain him while doing so.

The next day he says six guards at the center held him down, while medical staffers inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his throat, and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach – a process he called “traumatizing, both physically and psychologically”.

On 3 November, ICE then received permission from a federal judge to force-feed another hunger striker at Port Isabel, from Uzbekistan, federal court records show. DHS says the Uzbek man has not been subjected to the practice, however.

blocks.caption: The Port Isabel detention center in Los Fresnos, Texas. Photograph: Verónica G Cárdenas/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: On Wednesday night, after weeks of communications, Cora Perez was suddenly transferred to another detention center in Texas. His relative says neither of them were alerted to any plans to transfer him, or a reason for it.
DHS did not specify why Cora Perez was transferred, adding that ICE makes custody determinations on a “case-by-case” basis based on “various factors”.

The revelations come as ICE’s detention practices continue to come under fire amid allegations of mistreatment, and as an increasing number of sporadic hunger strikes have been breaking out in ICE facilities across the country.

The two men’s cases in Texas, revealed here for the first time, are some of the most recent instances of government lawyers seeking a federal judge’s permission, as required by ICE policy, and receiving the go-ahead to force-feed detained hunger strikers. The Guardian’s reporting is based on court records, interviews, dozens of messages exchanged and an interview conducted with Cora Perez via a facility phone. It further reveals how the Trump administration is increasingly obtaining such court orders to force-feed detained immigrants, a secretive practice widely condemned as torture by human rights organizations and medical ethics groups.

Detainees driven to hunger strike are typically using it as a last resort to protest against poor conditions and the Trump administration’s preference for arrest and prolonged detention while their civil immigration cases proceed through the system.

Cora Perez said detention center staff inserted the feeding tube and left it in his body, a not uncommon practice, according to experts, and introduced nutrition – first a “clear liquid”, followed by a “milky liquid”, he recalled – through the tube twice more that day, before he cracked and said he broke his hunger strike, citing what he called “horrific torture”. He began voluntarily drinking nutritional shakes the following day, he said.

“ICE does not hold back on anything, and they do anything they want, like we have seen, even killing their own US citizens,” he wrote to the Guardian, referring to the fatal shootings of Renee Good by an ICE officer and Alex Pretti by a border patrol officer in January of this year during Trump’s pivotal immigration crackdown on Minneapolis.

blocks.caption: Children look at posters honoring Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good, shot dead by federal agents in Minneapolis in January. Photograph: Tim Evans/Reuters

blocks.text: Detained hunger strikers subjected to involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding, have rarely spoken out about their cases or revealed their identities, much less while still detained. Cora Perez’s messages offer a rare glimpse at conditions inside a detention center’s restricted medical unit where hunger strikers and suicidal detainees are held.

“They just took [the Uzbek man] in an ambulance after [him] fainting in front of the medical lobby where they take our vitals, our weight and our temperature,” Cora said in an alarmed message last Monday morning.
The Uzbek man was returned the following day to the facility, Cora Perez said.
“I see him every day because I see him in the room in front of me, but they don’t let us talk to each other,” he added.

The Guardian independently confirmed the Uzbek’s man identity but is not publicly naming him, because efforts to contact him have been unsuccessful. The man arrived at the Mexico-US border in April 2022 and was released into the country while navigating his immigration case. He was arrested by border patrol officials in April of this year and placed in detention. The man does not appear to have any criminal record and DHS did not point to any criminal history.
In a statement, DHS said that after they received the court’s permission to force-feed the Uzbek man, he “has voluntarily taken in fluids and there has been NO force-feeding or forced hydration”.

Security operations at the sprawling Port Isabel facility in Los Fresnos, Texas are run by a private prison company, Akima Global Services, while healthcare is primarily handled by government workers.

blocks.caption: An examination area of the Port Isabel facility. Photograph: Verónica G Cárdenas/AFP via Getty Images

blocks.text: “ICE respects detainees’ rights to exercise self-expression and medical autonomy by refusing nourishment and medical care,” DHS said in a statement. “ICE Health Services Corps may provide involuntary medical treatment only to prevent imminent life-threatening harm or death. Medical staff may provide treatment only to medically stabilize the patient, bringing the detainee outside the imminent harm, incapacitation, or death.”

The US attorney’s office in the southern district of Texas, which represented ICE in its force-feeding request, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Virginia-headquartered Akima Global Services, and its parent company Nana Regional Corporation, based in Alaska, did not respond to a request for comment.

Force-feeding cases are shrouded in secrecy. After a detainee launches a hunger strike, ICE often sequesters them in medical isolation cells for monitoring, according to ICE’s detention standards. DHS said that ICE continues to offer hunger strikers three meals per day.

After a certain period of not eating, which varies per case, ICE will request a federal judge’s permission to force-feed the hunger striker. Many court records, and sometimes entire court dockets, are sealed and hidden from public view. In Cora Perez and the Uzbek man’s cases, like in others, they did not have any legal representation to challenge the force-feeding requests.

The Guardian found at least five instances in which ICE requested permission to force-feed hunger strikers in Port Isabel since January 2025. The federal judge who ruled on Cora Perez and the Uzbek man, Rolando Olvera, has similarly ordered in at least three other cases, records show. Olvera’s judicial assistant said the court had no comment for this article.

ICE is known to have requested permission to force-feed at least 21 detainees across the US since January 2025, the Guardian found, but the number is likely higher since an unknown number of records and dockets remain sealed, unsearchable and not feasible to locate. Most of the cases coinciding with the second Trump administration and tracked by the Guardian are in Texas and Florida, with others in Georgia, Arizona and Washington state. Under the Biden administration, ICE force-feeding requests were also made in Louisiana and California.

Amy Zeidan, an emergency medicine physician based in Atlanta and an expert on healthcare in immigration detention, said force-feeding hunger strikers can amount to “torture”, and lead to significant psychological distress. She also said it is a violation of medical ethics.

“Essentially it’s like inserting a straw into your nose,” Zeidan said. “You have a gag reflex, so most times people will gag, and that’s really uncomfortable. And people will even vomit repeatedly if it continues to irritate their gag reflex.”
Zeidan added that the forceful insertion of a feeding tube can lead to the swelling of the nostrils and the throat, and even tear them, leading to bleeding.

“It is like torture – somebody is doing a painful procedure to you that you don’t consent to,” Zeidan added. “Autonomy is a fundamental principle of medical ethics. We can’t do something to patients if they don’t want to, even if we think it’s good for them.”

There are numerous cells and rooms inside the Port Isabel medical unit, including isolation cells and shared rooms for ill detainees, according to Cora Perez. In recent weeks, there were five people in the Port Isabel medical isolation cells used for hunger striking or suicidal detainees, he added. He described the cells as “practically freezing”, constantly surveilled with a security camera, and with just a bed, toilet and sink. As well as himself, he says he observed the Uzbek man, a Middle Eastern man, a “tall” eastern European man and a Black man of unknown nationality in the isolation cells. Unit detainees are escorted by facility staff to showers and sometimes receive yard and television access, he said.

blocks.caption: A security guard at Port Isabel. Photograph: Verónica G Cárdenas/AFP via Getty Images

blocks.text: Cora Perez worries for the other detainees. The Black man, whose identity or nationality he does not know, seems to have “serious mental health problems”, Cora Perez observed.
“He harms himself and spends the night yelling and hitting the door, and does not let anyone sleep,” he said.

The Guardian has independently confirmed the eastern European and Middle Eastern men’s identities, but is not publicly naming them because efforts to contact them have been unsuccessful. DHS did not comment on the other men inside the medical isolation unit, saying they could not comment without the Guardian providing their identities.

Cora Perez had left his son and parents in Cuba and requested asylum at the Mexico-US border in 2023, according to a relative who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity due to fear of retaliation by immigration authorities. Cora Perez went to live with the relative in Florida, where he worked in maintenance at a hotel and as a food delivery worker, he said.

In March 2025, Cora Perez was arrested by local police and later convicted of two misdemeanors, including “breach of peace” and “obstructing an officer without violence”, according to local records. He was sentenced to two months in jail, his relative said. But ICE placed a hold on him and as he was being released in June 2025, immigration officials took him into custody – a common system – and soon transferred him to the Adelanto detention center, a privately-run facility in California.

Days in Adelanto turned to weeks, then months, then a over year, according to a federal court order denying one of his petitions requesting his release. His multiple requests to immigration and ordinary federal courts for release from detention, while he fights his asylum case, have been unsuccessful.

“All his claims will be heard by an immigration judge, and he will receive due process. This administration will not ignore the rule of law,” DHS said. “Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the US.”
In August, he stopped eating to protest against his protracted detention.

“I have spent two birthdays behind ICE’s bars,” he wrote. “The reasons I did the hunger strike in Adelanto are for my political asylum, for the time I have spent detained, [and] because I have a 14-year-old son who is starving to death in Cuba because he does not have my help.”
“Also due to the mistreatment by the officials,” he added.

Cora Perez did not tell his family about the hunger strike, so as not to further worry them. It was not until he was transferred to Port Isabel in late September that he confessed to his relative he had been on a prolonged hunger strike.
“He doesn’t share details so that I won’t get upset or worry,” the relative said in a phone interview.

blocks.caption: The barbed-wire fence at Port Isabel. Photograph: Verónica G Cárdenas/Reuters

blocks.text: Cora Perez’s mother, who is in Cuba, “does not know anything, because she is sick, and with his detention she has gotten worse”, the relative added, between tears. “I don’t want her nor his grandmother to know anything about it,” the relative added.

On October 30, the federal prosecutors requested permission for ICE to forcibly feed and hydrate Cora Perez. Hours later, a federal judge approved the procedures without hearing from Cora Perez. Cora Perez told the Guardian in various instances he felt it was unfair he was not given the opportunity to present his case to the judge before the judge approved his force-feeding.

“It’s very disturbing because the judge is basically making a decision on information that is only provided by one side,” said Linus Chan, a professor of clinical law and the director of the detainee rights clinic at the University of Minnesota law school. “That just seems ridiculous.”
Cora Perez was force-fed the following day, he said in his messages and in a phone call, adding that he did not physically resist because he “had seen a lot of mistreatment of others detained”.
“[ICE does] what they want with us, whatever they want, because a federal judge gave them permission,” he added. “I have suffered on the island [of Cuba] and now at the hands of ICE.”

After asking Cora Perez about DHS’s denials that he was force-fed, he repeated that he was. “Brother, ICE says and does whatever they want. They deny, punish, retaliate and do everything at their own will. They have even sent Cubans to Africa,” he said.

The number of people detained by ICE has soared under the Trump administration. And due to policy and legal changes, tens of thousands of people are forced to stay in detention for long periods while they fight their immigration cases.
Chan, from the University of Minnesota, says prolonged detention and delays in their cases lead to logical conclusion. “That’s exactly when people protest,” he said.
“And the only form of protest, for many of these people, is a hunger strike,” he said.
As Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown continues and people are detained as a first resort while their cases play out, Chan said: “Hunger strikes will become more common.”

articles.title: Can German auto manufacturing recover after Mercedes and VW cuts?
articles.summary: German automakers are pulling back on investments at home, sparking fresh anxiety about the auto sector's future. Some industry watchers think there is still a narrow window to stem the decline. But…

image.caption: Mercedes-Benz has halted all further investments in German manufacturing for the time being and is also weighing plant closuresImage: Bernd Weißbrod/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Mercedes-Benz's announcement last week that it would halt further investments at its factories in Germany has added to the sense that the country's best automaking days are behind it.
In a written interview for staff, production chief Michael Schiebe noted how the running costs of German plants are far too high.
Schiebe added that the automaker is "now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure."
The decision came one day after Volkswagen (VW), Europe's largest carmaker, said it was shelving plans to modernize its massive Wolfsburg plant.
Can crisis reinvent the car again?
German auto industry faces restructuring

Germany's auto sector is in a deep crisis, amid fierce rivalry from ambitious Chinese automakers. VW alone is looking to cut 100,000 jobs globally by 2030, while four of its German factories are earmarked for possible closure.
Yet, many auto analysts doubt this really marks the beginning of the end for car making in the country.

"We have to admit that a third of our capacity [in German plants] is overcapacity and that needs to be cut," Thomas Puls, senior economist for transport and infrastructure at the Cologne Institute for Economic Research (IW Köln), told DW. "This will hurt a lot."

A report last month by Munich-based consultancy Roland Bergeragreed that domestic automaking needs an urgent "reset," but predicted that Germany could still "preserve a sustainably profitable core of automotive value creation."
In other words, car making in Germany may shrink, but what remains could be leaner, more specialized and more profitable.

blocks.caption: In Germany, Mercedes has three assembly plants and seven facilities that manufacture drivetrains and componentsImage: Axel Schmidt/REUTERS

blocks.text: Unions dig in amid fight for survival

Many doomsayers overlook the fact that Mercedes' investment halt is tied to tough negotiations with unions over cutting labor costs at its German plants. This includes scrapping the 35-hour workweek. The investment freeze could be lifted if a deal is reached.
Even so, Achim Kampker, an electric mobility engineering professor at RWTH Aachen University, sees the investment cuts as more than a negotiating tactic.
Kampker compared China's lightning-fast industrial strategy with Germany's, which he said was "too slow," as excessive bureaucracy and complex business structures prevent value creation.
"We need to become faster, more innovative and significantly more productive," Kampker told DW.
China's EV-makers can bring a new model to market in around 20 months, versus 48 to 60 months for Germany, according to Roland Berger. Plus, the Chinese have a 30% cost advantage.
Production costs at German plants are also much higher — between €3,500 ($3,840) and €5,000 per vehicle — than in Eastern Europe, where they range from €2,000 to €2,500.

blocks.caption: Mercedes plans more than 40 model launches by next year — a growing share will be built outside GermanyImage: Joan Cros/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Does Germany have a 'false sense of security?'

A separate report by consultancy PwC in September noted that despite German carmakers being well managed, well capitalized and knowing exactly what is coming, they may have a "false sense of security."
PwC said Germany needs to focus on four areas to ensure its auto industry is "future-fit" to compete with China.

These include splitting its internal combustion engine (ICE) business from the electric vehicle (EV) business, investing bumper ICE profits into those new technologies, redesigning workplace culture and training, and leveraging existing partnerships with Chinese automakers and US tech firms.
"The future viability of the German automotive industry depends significantly on decisions made in the next 12 to 18 months," wrote Harald Wimmer, global and German automotive leader at PwC Germany.
With the transition to EVs, some predict that automaking will become part of a much larger global electronics sector, which Germany must exploit.

Wimmer noted how top Chinese automakers were already benchmarking themselves against consumer electronics giants. These include smartphone maker Xiaomi, which now also produces around 400,000 EVs per year.
"Anyone who continues to base their competitive framework solely on their own industry is making a mistake that cannot be corrected once it becomes apparent," he warned.
Production remains resilient despite decline
Despite all the doom and gloom, car production within Germany is holding up pretty well.

Domestic manufacturing sits around 12% lower than pre-pandemic levels. This year, however, the auto sector is on course to meet a December estimate of 4.11 million vehicles, just 1% lower than last year, according to the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA).
IW Köln's Puls thinks German automakers must now avoid a trap Italy fell into in the early 2000s when its national auto champion, Fiat, struggled with profitability.

In Italy, "the politics and the unions blocked any attempt by Fiat to cut overcapacity," Puls told DW. "What's the result? They have a capacity of 1.1 to 1.2 million cars and utilization of about 250,000."
Last year, those same Italian plants built just 214,000 passenger cars, according to the FIM Cisl trade union, the fewest since 1954.
Analysts call for faster reform
For Germany, the issue isn't a lack of expertise or ambition; it's that reforms to huge industries often get weighed down by caution and red tape.

As the country's auto giants try to push through painful cuts, RWTH Aachen University's Kampker warned that if they fail to address their shortcomings, "we will see more production sites closing and a substantial shift of industrial investment and employment away from Germany."
"There is still an opportunity to reverse this trend, but the window of opportunity is narrowing," Kampker concluded.

articles.title: Global stock markets slump as Anthropic IPO fails to stem AI sell-off
articles.summary: Asian markets on track for their worst week since 2020, with European and US stocks also way down

blocks.text: Global stock markets have slumped as Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies.

Asian stock markets were on track for their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell on Friday. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chipmaker TSMC down about 6%.

In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.
European stock markets were heading for their worst week since March, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.3% in the first 90 minutes.
The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by over 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.

Anthropic’s shares jumped 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the frontier AI firm began. But they were heading for losses on Friday, down 6% at $91.30, falling back towards the IPO price of $83.

Anthropic’s floation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.

“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”
after newsletter promotion
Britain’s FTSE 100 share index hit a five-month low on Friday morning. It has dropped by 4.8% this week, and is heading for its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.

articles.title: California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state
articles.summary:
Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded

Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive…

blocks.text: Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.

Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.

blocks.caption: A large wave pours over the seawall in Pacifica. Photograph: Fred Greaves/Reuters

blocks.text: Nearly 72,000 people have been evacuated from areas of Odisha in eastern India as Tropical Cyclone Akvan approaches land. Akvan is expected to make landfall on Friday between Narsapur and Puri, prompting cyclone warnings from the India Meteorological Department for north Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and south Odisha coasts. Peak wind gusts are expected to reach 70mph, with rainfall totals through Friday and Saturday potentially exceeding 200mm for northern coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.

blocks.caption: Fishers carry a boat to a safer place along the shore before the expected landfall of Tropical Cyclone Akvan near Gopalpur in Odisha, India. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: Following a Yellow Level 2 severe thunderstorm warning by the South African Weather Service on Tuesday, torrential rainfall and large hail were reported across parts of Johannesburg. The storms triggered flash flooding and caused infrastructure damage in the township of Soweto. One person died, while another remains missing after the severe storms.

articles.title: A Montrealer died in Istanbul. Authorities blame food poisoning but what we found suggests something else
articles.summary: A young Canadian woman travelled to Turkey after graduating from medical school. In her last days there, she fell ill and died within hours. Authorities there blame food poisoning, but a joint…
articles.byline: Michelle Gagnon, Jacaudrey Charbonneau, Judith Plamondon

image.caption: Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino visited Capadoccia, Turkey, in 2025 as part of a trip celebrating her recent graduation from medical school. During that trip, the 24-year-old Montrealer died suddenly in Istanbul. (Submitted by Deveaux-Cattino family)

blocks.text: Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino, a healthy 24-year-old Montrealer, died suddenly in Istanbul on June 17, 2025.
A Turkish autopsy report concluded the cause of death was food poisoning.
But for her family, that doesn't add up.
A joint investigation into Deveaux-Cattino's death by Enquête and the fifth estate revealed a different poison at work and 12 similar deaths.
The recent medical school graduate had decided to celebrate by taking a trip with a few of her closest friends.
"She'd never been to Turkey," said her sister, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino. "She thought it was a super beautiful, vibrant country."
The group hit the tourist trail and its highlights, including the requisite balloon ride in Cappadocia.
Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino had never been to Turkey before her trip in 2025, says her sister, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino. ‘She thought it was a super beautiful, vibrant country.’ (Radio-Caanda)
With only two days to go, Bérengère and one of her friends headed for Istanbul, a city she'd longed to visit.

items: Watch the full documentary, "The Invisible Killer," from the fifth estate on YouTube or CBC-TV on Friday at 9 p.m.

blocks.text: They checked into Room 108 at the Seven Days Hotel and went straight out to explore. They soaked up the sights and street food, then settled down for a proper meal, a chicken casserole followed by Turkish tea and baklava.
The next morning, they woke violently ill.
Laurie recalls the final days

The details of those final days come from Laurie, the woman who travelled to Istanbul with Bérengère. What happened on that trip left her traumatized and we've agreed to protect her identity and not use her real name.
She said that within minutes of waking, Bérengère was throwing up.
"Then I started feeling unwell," Laurie said, "and suddenly we were taking turns running to the bathroom to vomit until we realized that whatever it was, it wasn't just going to pass."
They called the front desk and an ambulance took them to hospital.
‘My sister is younger than me,’ said Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino, right. ‘I’d never imagined a life without her.’ (Submitted by Deveaux-Cattino family)
'Things aren't going well'
That same day, across the ocean in Montreal, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino saw her screen light up: Laurie was FaceTiming her.

"I thought: 'This isn't normal. Something's off. This is going to be bad news,'" said Deveaux-Cattino. "She says 'Élo, we're in the hospital in Istanbul, and things aren't going well. I've been told to contact the family.'"
Deveaux-Cattino and her father, Henri Cattino, scrambled to find flights to Istanbul. While waiting for their connection in Paris, Deveaux-Cattino called the embassy.
"I said: 'Please, can you tell me if my sister has died?'" said Deveaux-Cattino. ”And she said: 'I'm very sorry, Éléonore, but your sister is dead.'"
Three days into their trip to Istanbul in November 2025, the Böcek family from Hamburg fell ill. Five days later, all four family members were dead, poisoned by phosphine gas. (@ismailsaymaz/X)
The Böcek family
The Deveaux-Cattinos repatriated Bérengère's body and asked the Quebec coroner's office to examine it. They buried their daughter and sister without confirmation of the cause of death.
As they waited for answers from Turkey, the family speculated about what else could explain Bérengère's death: Organ trafficking? Alcohol poisoning? Medical malpractice?
Then, in November, as we were investigating, a diplomatic source texted with a tip that pointed to an entirely different explanation.
"A family of four has just died in Istanbul. Watch this report."
The Böceks, a Turkish-German family from Hamburg, were visiting Istanbul. Their hotel was blocks from where Bérengère and Laurie stayed. All four fell ill and died within days of each other.

Investigators initially suspected food poisoning there, too. But within days, authorities concluded that another poison had been at work: aluminum phosphide, a highly toxic agricultural pesticide used to kill rodents and insects.
The 'bomb'

Exterminators call aluminum phosphide "the bomb." It is used in pellet form. Once the pellets are exposed to air, they release phosphine gas. Exterminators say that when placed in a sealed room, the gas kills every living, breathing thing within 72 hours. In Turkey, it's illegal to use in urban areas.
But, like all big cities, Istanbul has a bedbug problem.
Safe extermination of bedbugs
Exterminator Birkan Cihan said he can barely keep up with calls from desperate home and hotel owners. Some ask whether he treats bedbugs with "gas." He doesn't.
"We tell them their neighbours could die from it, and that they could, too. But they say: 'We have no choice, it's the only thing that works,'" Cihan said
The phosphine gas these pellets emit is so potent and volatile that it can spread through a building, even if the area being treated is sealed.
In the case of the Böcek family, fumigation in the neighbouring room was determined to be what killed all four of them.
Investigations by Enquête and the fifth estate have found similar cases. In 2012, two sisters from Quebec, Audrey and Noémi Bélanger, died of phosphine poisoning in Thailand.
In 2012, two sisters from Quebec, Audrey and Noémi Bélanger, died of phosphine poisoning in Thailand. (Submitted by Bélanger family)
'That doesn't make any sense'

Just before Christmas 2025, the Deveaux-Cattinos received the autopsy report from Turkey. It concluded that food poisoning caused Bérengère's death. Unconvinced, they handed the report to the Quebec coroner's office.

"The coroner here ran some tests, and she couldn't confirm that food poisoning was the cause of death because, usually, there are signs of intestinal irritation," Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino said. "There were none in my sister's case."
We showed the Turkish autopsy report to another Quebec pathologist. Although not authorized to speak publicly, he also questioned the autopsy's conclusions.

"Two young, healthy women who end up in the hospital with food poisoning — OK, I'll buy that. But to die of it so quickly, without any signs of bloody diarrhea or other complications, that doesn't make any sense."
Turkish freelance journalist Ayse Adanali covered the story of the death of the Böcek family in Istanbul in 2025. (Radio-Canada)
Women and children
In Turkey, we started working with Ayse Adanali, a freelance Turkish journalist who'd covered the Böcek story.
Together, we documented nearly 30 cases of phosphine poisoning, including a dozen deaths, since 2023 in Turkey.

Some were tourists, like the two Dutch teenagers found dead by their father in their Istanbul hotel room in August 2025. But most of the victims were Turkish, like Karan Yazıcı, a three-year-old boy poisoned in Istanbul in April 2025 following a fumigation in the neighbouring apartment.

The majority of the victims are women and children. Members of the same family were often poisoned together. While some survived, others died. In most cases, food poisoning was initially blamed for making them sick.
'This is not food poisoning'
Şebnem Korur Fincancı is a human rights activist, professor emeritus and leading forensic pathologist in Turkey.
She's studied aluminum phosphide and knows how difficult it is to identify victims poisoned by phosphine gas.
Turkish forensic pathologist Şebnem Korur Fincancı has studied aluminum phosphide and knows how difficult it is to identify victims poisoned by phosphine gas. (Radio-Canada)
She'd never heard about Bérengère; her death had not been covered by Turkish media.
"This is not food poisoning," she said after reading the Turkish autopsy report.
"I don't think that this is food poisoning because there is no story of diarrhea, only throwing up."
She added that the timing of Bérengère's decline suggests food poisoning couldn't be the culprit.
"Rather, it is the pesticide poisoning."

Fincancı sees one undeniable detail in this report, a finding common to all victims of phosphine gas poisoning she's examined: something called metabolic acidosis, which increases the levels of acidity in the body.
"There is the metabolic acidosis, which also indicates the pesticide intoxication," she said. 'It is one of the main findings of these kinds of cases."
She believes there could be more cases of phosphine poisoning than currently reported.
"With all these misdiagnoses, we have to consider the situation."
Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino and her friend, Laurie, stayed at the Seven Days Hotel in Istanbul. (Radio-Canada)
150 bites
We scoured hundreds of Google and Tripadvisor reviews for the Seven Days Hotel to see if they'd had a bedbug problem around the time of Bérengère and Laurie's stay.
One stood out: A tourist claiming he'd been bitten 150 times during his stay in June 2025.
We tracked him down. He confirmed he stayed in Room 107, the room next door to where the two women stayed 10 days later.
The windows in those two rooms open onto each other.
That left one critical question: Had Room 107 been treated after his stay? And, if so, with what?
We contacted hotel manager Bahattin Demir. He remembered Bérengère and Laurie and had gone to the hospital after they'd been admitted.
We told him about the tourist in Room 107 and asked him whether extermination work in that room could have killed Bérengère.
"I don't think so, because if it was that product, I'm sure that, you know, everybody would have this problem," he said.
Inside Room 108 at the Seven Days Hotel where Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino and Laurie stayed. (Radio-Canada)
He said exterminators spray the rooms in the hotel monthly. He offered to contact them and find out what product they use, but then wrote back, referring us to them for more details.
The extermination company is called Wolves.
A contact called them for us. We're protecting her identity because undercover work can lead to jail time in Turkey.
Posing as an Air BnB owner in Istanbul's Fatih district, she claimed to be struggling with bedbugs.
The employee was cautious on the phone.
He didn't name the product specifically, but his detailed description is similar to how aluminum phosphide is used.
"For 72 hours, nobody goes in, the doors are locked and nothing living enters."

items: Deaths of Quebec women in Thailand may have been caused by pesticide
Phosphine pesticide used to kill bedbugs causes Fort McMurray baby's death

blocks.text: We called Wolves for an interview. The employee who answered the phone was not authorized to speak, but denied using aluminum phosphide.
Neither the hospital that treated Bérengère nor the Forensic Medical Centre where her autopsy was performed replied to our inquiries.
The tourism police similarly declined our interview request.

Going over notes Laurie had shared, we noticed she and Bérengère had left the window open the first night. But the next evening, to avoid being woken by the call to prayer, they closed it and turned on the air conditioning. And that was the night they got sick.
We asked pathologist Şebnem Korur Fincancı whether phosphine gas residue could build up in air conditioners.
"Of course," she said.
'Those who are gone'

The Böceks' case went to trial in June 2026. The defendants were charged with criminal negligence causing the deaths of this family of four. The ruling came down within days. The owners of the extermination company were found guilty and sentenced to 18 years in prison. The hotel owner and employees received 12 to 13 years.
While awaiting the verdict, the paternal grandfather, Yilmaz Böcek, commented that even the stiffest penalty could never bring back his children and grandchildren.
"Those who are gone never come back."
Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino wants Bérengère to be remembered.
"My sister is younger than me. I'd never imagined a life without her. We used to be two against the world … now I'm all alone," she said.
"But I'm stubborn. And since she can no longer speak, I'll speak for her. I'll never let her go."

In the summer of 2026, the government of Canada added a new entry to its travel advisory for Turkey, alerting travellers to "cases of poisoning linked to the use of chemical pesticides in tourist accommodations in Istanbul."
After this story first aired on Oct. 15, 2026, Turkish consular officials contacted us, confirming the investigation into Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino's death in Istanbul remains open.

articles.title: Sunrise on the Reaping may be a prequel, but it's the worst way to start The Hunger Games
articles.summary: The framing of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping as a painful, nihilistic and unrelentingly dour backstory for a single character makes it a deeply strange movie when viewed as a standalone…

image.caption: Joseph Zada as a young Haymitch Abernathy in a still from The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping. (Murray Close/Lionsgate)

blocks.text: Entertainment·REVIEW

The framing of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping as a painful, nihilistic and unrelentingly dour backstory for a single character makes it a deeply strange movie when viewed as a standalone feature.
Latest chapter in dystopian franchise is more focused on backstory than story — and is almost absurdly morose
There is perhaps no worse instalment of The Hunger Games franchise to get started with than the new prequel, Sunrise on the Reaping.

That should be a silly statement on face value. With five movies in the young-adult, Battle Royale-esque series already out — four of them following "girl on fire" Katniss Everdeen's quest to stop the dictatorial Capitol government from pitting randomly selected kids against one another in modern gladiator matches — you'd think the audience is coming in fairly well versed.

So with Sunrise on the Reaping simply moving back and telling the story of how one grizzled character once competed in a blood-soaked tournament of his own, why does The Hunger Games need to hold your hand?

Well, because its creator said that was the goal. According to director Francis Lawrence, making Reaping function as a genuine entry point into the series works for both new and old audiences, independent of their experience with other films — a claim to craft a functional and entertaining midbrow action movie with new faces, but also to make it stand entirely on its own merits.
It's a lofty pair of goals — the first of which Reaping actually more or less meets as a relatively strong entry in the overcrowded, clichéd YA post-apocalyptic canon.
But in confronting the second goal, it ends up either failing outright; or barely passes by crafting one of the more bizarrely morose entries in the "chosen one" narrative field of all time.

Instead of introducing the undauntable, constantly thwarted heroine Katniss, we follow the battle-scarred side character of Haymitch Abernathy — whose function has long been to be unhappy — and are told what made him so titillatingly broken when fans first met him.
That might be interesting for those who have followed along from the beginning and are just hungry for more.

But to those without any insight into who eventually triumphs over whom decades after all this unrewarding, unrelenting, unromantic failure, Reaping is something else. Its framing as a painful, almost universally nihilistic and unrelentingly dour backstory for a single character makes it a deeply strange movie when viewed as a standalone feature.

Played in the original Hunger Games by Woody Harrelson as a grizzled, traumatized veteran of the games, Haymitch is here taken on by Joseph Zada. It's 24 years ahead of the events of the first movie, on the eve of something called the Second Quarter Quell.

It is a requisitely arcane term for a pivotal Hunger Games competition, one that those following along know ended in even more bloodshed and tears than is normal — and somehow left an older, meaner Haymitch looking on in fiery-eyed fury when the corrupt, manipulative government presented him with doctored, propagandistic footage of it in the first movie.
For those out of the know, though, this movie could still end in either heroic victory or heroic martyrization.

Those expectations seem even more likely as we go through the typical setup: music video shots of Haymitch telling his girl Lenore (Whitney Peak) in a slightly southern accent that he'll never let her go; Haymitch saving her from his fate by selflessly setting himself up "tribute" for his district — the saddest, rinky-dinkiest, underdoggiest district in the whole state of Panem; and his ironic slow-clapping at the impassive President Snow (Ralph Fiennes) looking down at the moaning and dying young combatants in the arena below.
Ralph Fiennes as President Snow in a still from The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping. (Lionsgate)

These are all expected and solidly executed moral and narrative markers for the tragic or triumphant formula to work off. They get more narrative juice once the real plot starts, as the mysterious Beetee Latier (Kelvin Harrison Jr.) sneaks out from the arena compound's shadows to present Haymitch with a plan to take the Capitol down from the inside, forgo trying to win the competition, and try to stop the ruling class from exploiting them.
There's only one problem: if Haymitch does this, he's not getting out alive.

Of course, this being the backstory for a character still alive in other Hunger Games movies precludes that eventuality. But instead of ruining the experience for those who know the broad-strokes ending, it only diminishes it: what was once compellingly mysterious, hinted-at trauma in Haymitch's rear-mirror moves from imagination and suggestion to about 30 minutes of screaming, montage-based alcoholism and more tiny coffins than a Dracula-themed dollhouse.

Where the maudlin collage of trauma in Reaping's back half might harden and simplify old fans' relationship with Haymitch, it is simply bizarre for a newcomer. Instead of a story about victory over fascism — either real, performative or pyrrhic — we get a cruel rug-pull that lacks both a cohesive emotional framing and message.

items: Club Kid is one of TIFF's best. It might make you cry
Ebenezer review: Merry Christmas, Johnny Depp! Is this your comeback yet?

blocks.text: A fuzzy theme around learned helplessness is there — the "implicit submission" of the masses obeying a minority explained by philosopher David Hume, as The Hunger Games author Suzanne Collins has said. And, sure, the citizens in Reaping fail to realize the power they have to fight back.

But aside from a trite, tacked-on ending — whose emotional weight hinges entirely upon the assumption you know the triumphs Katniss Everdeen will achieve — the rest is just punishment for punishment's sake.

The dragged-out, morose portrayal of the pointlessness of Haymitch's existence works to explain his later anger — a useful tidbit if you ever make it to the first film. But aside from the novelty of a story refusing you redemption or fulfillment, there's little else for those making their way into the tale.
With the real end to Sunrise on the Reaping being The Hunger Games, you might as well start there. Or not start at all.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Race to be next UN secretary general exposes divisions among world powers
articles.summary:
Debate about dominance of permanent five members could reignite if major powers block Costa Rican frontrunner

The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment…

blocks.text: The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the big powers. If so, the setback will reignite a debate about the dominance of the permanent five (P5) members at the United Nations.

Rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica, has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July. Each member goes down the list of candidates, casting an “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion” vote for each candidate.

Despite countries not being required to reveal how they voted, it is thought Grynspan’s candidature has been resisted by Russia and the US, two of the five permanent security council members that can ultimately wield a veto against a candidate. Knowledge among the security council delegations of how countries are voting is down to private intelligence, leaks and a process of elimination.

The intensive lobbying over the job has spread across the globe, but Friday is especially important since the poll is slated to differentiate the voting of the P5 from the 10 elected members (E10) of the security council. To be recommended as secretary general to the UN general assembly, a candidate needs nine votes and no vetoes. In Friday’s colour-coded secret ballot, the P5 will cast red ballots and the E10 white.
One diplomat said: “The electoral system means it is important how many votes you win, but equally how many of certain votes you don’t lose.”

blocks.caption: Polarisation has also hampered the incumbent secretary general, António Guterres. Photograph: Ted Aljibe/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: The protracted 140-day deadlock confirms the polarisation that has hampered the incumbent secretary general, António Guterres, but also belies claims the role is now an irrelevance.

Friday’s secret ballot may also reveal whether the United Arab Emirates’ campaign for its diplomat, Lana Nusseibeh, is about to blow up in its face due to the hostility to the UAE’s brand of active, commercially driven diplomacy, not just in Sudan, but also Somalia, Western Sahara, Libya and Yemen.

A late entrant, in the two straw polls in which she has contested so far, Nusseibeh secured only seven “encourage” votes, six “discourage” and two “no opinions”. This is despite prestigious big-power backing and her acknowledged personal diplomatic skills.

Nusseibeh has US and Russian backing. The French foreign ministry may have misgivings about the UAE, but Emmanuel Macron, the French president, travelled to the UAE in the midst of French riots to see the UAE president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and secure 100,000 metric tons of diesel a month.

blocks.caption: The UAE’s Lana Nusseibeh has US and Russian backing. Photograph: David Dee Delgado/Reuters

blocks.text: In the UK, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has kept his counsel, but he shares a Polish-Jewish refugee heritage with Grynspan and cannot be an admirer of the UAE’s human rights record or its evasion of EU sanctions on Russia. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has UAE connections from his time as mayor of Manchester, and Nusseibeh is a fellow alumnus of the University of Cambridge. At the UN she worked closely with the UK in an informal group called “Friends of the Future of the UN”.

Yet 68 British MPs, including the Labour chair of the international development select committee, Sarah Champion, last week signed a letter calling on Burnham to veto Nusseibeh, describing her as “a tainted and compromised figure”.

Some of the opposition to her from elected security council members is not wholly political. Latin American countries believe an informal rotation system means it is their turn to lead the UN. As a result Panama and Colombia, currently on the security council, will oppose her. China has also been supportive of this rotation principle.

But others deeply object to what they consider to be the UAE’s dollar diplomacy and preparedness to use its extraordinary wealth to exacerbate and exploit pre-existing divisions in a country to gain a commercial foothold. Somalia, for instance, has a seat on the Security Council, and its president, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, this week went on TV to accuse the UAE of buying ports, establishing military bases and supporting armed forces outside Somalia’s national security framework without federal approval.

It is also possible that Finland and Latvia, the two elected members with the greatest stake in Ukraine, are unimpressed that the UAE gave Vladimir Putin red carpet treatment when he visited Abu Dhabi in December 2023, nine months after the international criminal court had issued an arrest warrant for child trafficking. Greece, less engaged in Ukraine, may be more flexible.

Since the last poll, Nusseibeh has been to Bahrain, Britain and Pakistan, a clue as to where extra votes may be harvested. She also had a “thoughtful exchange” with Zeng Jixin, the Chinese ambassador to the UAE.

The two hurdles are whether someone so deep inside the UAE inner circle would have the courage in office to show true independence, and whether her active denials of UAE involvement in arming the RSF in Sudan leave her irretrievably tainted. From a Palestinian intellectual family, she insists she would make peace in Sudan her number one priority.

In the last ballot on 5 November, Grynspan won 12 votes in favour and three negative. But on 16 October – the only colour-coded ballot so far – which distinguishes between permanent and elected members – she received two discourage votes from permanent members, the equivalent of a veto. Nusseibeh had not joined the race at that point.

blocks.caption: Russia has opposed the Argentine candidate Rafael Grossi, objecting to his interventions over the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant in Ukraine. Photograph: Matthias Schräder/AP

blocks.text: In an administration as personalised as the US, it has been hard for Grynspan to gain influence, with many sensing that Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, is the key influencer.

Grynspan has been reluctant to make the fact she is Jewish a feature of her candidacy, but the election of a Jewish person to run the UN might be seen as something the US could embrace as transformative. Her age – she is 70 – could be considered a drawback among those calling for a younger generation to renew the institution.

Although there are other Latin American candidates, Grynspan is seen as a more viable candidate than her rival, the Argentine Rafael Grossi, the head of the UN weapons inspectorate. Russia has opposed Grossi, objecting to his interventions over the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant in Ukraine.
One way or the other, the logjam has to be broken soon.

articles.title: Iraq university’s removal of male professors teaching women sparks weeks of protests
articles.summary:
Al-Qadisiyah University’s move a sign of the country’s slide into a Taliban-like gender segregation, say activists

The removal of male professors teaching female students at a university in…
articles.byline: Ali Aziz, Maria Talal and Tom Levitt

blocks.text: The removal of male professors teaching female students at a university in southern Iraq has sparked protests and been criticised by activists as a Taliban-like gender segregation policy.

As many as 400 women are estimated to have joined protests over the past two weeks calling for the return of their professors at Al-Qadisiyah University in a move that appears to have surprised its administrators.

The university said the move was necessary to “prevent the mixing” of men and women and had been requested by the families of female students. But students said their families had known since before they enrolled that there were men on the teaching staff and supported their daughters’ protest.

Students said university bosses had mocked their protests and refused to discuss their concerns about the sudden loss of their academic supervisors. On social media, commentators also accused the women of seeking to keep male professors to “establish immoral relationships with them”.

“My classmates and I went to demonstrate, and the university president, Rahi al-Yasiri, blocked our path with his bodyguards, who then began making fun of us. He ordered them to take photographs of our faces, in an attempt to intimidate us and punish us later,” said Huda, 22, one of the female students.

Huda said the students tried to explain how men and women still worked together in society in Iraq. “Aren’t there doctors who treat both men and women? Why then do you prevent male professors from teaching us, too?” In response, Huda said Al-Yasiri replied: “Even if you hit your heads against the wall, I will not bring back the professors.”

The students said a large number of them were tied to graduation projects and research supervised by the professors. They said they had grown accustomed to their professors’ teaching methods, who also knew their students’ strengths and weaknesses, which made replacing them at this stage more complicated.
Female students said they had been told by the university that if they were not happy with the change, they should drop out.

An Iraqi-British feminist researcher, Balsam Mustafa, from the University of Cardiff, said the female students were “treated as if they are minors without the right to object to decisions affecting their academic lives”.

Mustafa said the removal of the male professors was a part of a worrying trend in women’s rights in the country, with “growing discussion about women’s clothing and chastity reflected in the celebration of female students who wear the abaya”.
An Iraqi lawyer and human rights activist, Israa Salman, said the restrictions on women was a “societal catastrophe”.

“Attempts are being made to suppress women’s talents and turn Iraqi society – a society that has produced remarkable minds and expertise, with women playing pioneering roles in many fields – into something resembling Kabul under Taliban rule.
“This contradicts Iraq’s constitution and the international treaties and conventions the country has signed and ratified,” said Salman.
Produced in collaboration with Jummar, an independent Iraqi media platform

articles.title: Myanmar ruling gives new relevance to genocide convention and is ‘full of messages’ for Israel
articles.summary:
Hailed as ‘a rare moment of justice’, judges’ decision sets out a roadmap for assessing the question of intent

The

blocks.text: The international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states.

In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused of committing genocide against a whole population group, especially when it comes to assessing the question of intent.
The lengthy judgment will have been read particularly carefully by Israel, the only other country currently before the ICJ accused of genocide.
It is also relevant to Germany, which has been brought before the court by Nicaragua on the accusation it has facilitated and failed to prevent genocide in Gaza.

“I think it’s a judgment that brings the genocide convention alive,” said Philippe Sands, a leading human rights lawyer who was part of the Gambian legal team. “It gives the convention practical, real meaning. And if the alternative view had been taken, the convention would essentially become a dead letter.”

Amnesty International’s secretary general, Agnès Callamard, called the ruling “a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families”. But it was also an assertion of humanitarian law in an increasingly lawless world.

“This is a good day for international law. We needed it,” said Dr Iva Vukušić, an assistant professor in international History at Utrecht University and a war crimes expert. “It is really important, clarifying a lot of law, and that’s going to be very helpful going forward.”

There will be a spillover from this ruling to its sister tribunal in The Hague, the international criminal court (ICC), providing a benchmark for when genocide charges could be made against individual perpetrators.

The Trump administration, instinctively hostile to international legal institutions, is also watching critically. The US ambassador to the UN told the ICJ before this judgment not to “lower the legal threshold for proving genocide” lest it be “weaponised” against US and allied soldiers.
The court did not directly lower the standard for demonstrating genocide, and the Gambia – which brought the case to The Hague – did not ask it to.

The judges kept the existing benchmark for judging genocide intent as the “only reasonable inference” of Myanmar’s actions and referred extensively to prior case law. But it went a long way towards clarifying how that standard should be applied in assessing atrocity crimes committed by states.

Before this case, only Serbia had faced the charge of genocide at the ICJ, in cases brought by Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the Bosnian ruling in 2007, Belgrade was found to have failed to prevent the 1995 genocide in Srebrenica, but in both cases it was cleared of committing the genocide directly.

The new ICJ judgment finds the Myanmar military directly responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, a Muslim minority targeted in a ferocious counterinsurgency campaign that reached its peak in 2017.

In assessing the Myanmar campaign, the ICJ looked not just at the death toll of about 10,000 in assessing the scale of the atrocities, but at the total Rohingya population targeted in northern Rakhine state, 815,000 people. Significantly, it cast its net wider than just the death toll, considering mental damage done to the survivors, particularly victims of sexual violence, and the impact on reproduction in the Rohingya community.

Most importantly, the ICJ judgment provided a guide to interpreting the standard set by Serbian cases, in which a finding of genocide could be made only if there were not other plausible motives for mass killing.

In this judgment, the court ruled that Myanmar could have had other motives, such as the desire to displace or punish the Rohingya population, but that those motives could exist alongside genocidal intent. The judges said genocidal intent was the “only reasonable inference” from the “totality” of evidence.

In justifying that conclusion the judges pointed to several factors that international law experts say are relevant to the Gaza case, which is now hearing written pleadings and is expected to take at least another three years.

The common factors include the targeting of children, which the court described as striking at the “foundation” of the Rohingya as a group – the ICJ said up to 2,109 Rohingya children under the age of five had been killed, while more than 5,000 Palestinian children under five years old have been killed in the Gaza war.

Another incriminating factor cited by the court was the “bulldozing and large-scale terrain clearance” after the destruction of villages, followed by “rapid construction” including security installations, which has been the hallmark of Israeli army occupation of over 60% of the Gaza Strip.

“It’s full of messages for Israel,” said William Schabas, an international law professor and expert on genocide at Middlesex University. “There are obvious differences, of course, the evidence will be different, but if you exchanged the word Myanmar with Israel, you wouldn’t have to change much in the judgment.”

The fact that there were six dissenting voices on the bench suggested that substantial parts of the majority’s reasoning were not beyond dispute, and lawyers involved in the case cautioned that it did not necessarily mean that the same bench would find Israel guilty of genocide in Gaza. But the same lawyers added that the opposite was almost certainly true. If this case had failed, the case brought by South Africa against Israel would have been all but over.

articles.title: ‘Everyone struggled for this justice’: tears in court as Rohingya vindicated in Myanmar genocide ruling
articles.summary:
Relief in the immediate aftermath of a landmark ruling, but what happens next is in the hands of governments around the world

There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands…

blocks.text: There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh as the scattered communities of Rohingya watched the UN’s top court rule the Myanmar military had committed genocide against them.

For almost a decade, the Rohingya have awaited this moment; recognition from the international court of justice (ICJ) that Myanmar in 2017 intentionally tried to destroy the mostly Muslim minority group through a campaign of mass killings and rape. More than 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 700,000 fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.

By the time they spilled into the court’s halls, the relief was evident. A Rohingya community leader threw a big thumbs up as he left the courtroom and others immediately took out their phones to call family in the refugee camps.

Salma, 30, a Rohingya survivor who lost family members in the 2017 genocide, said: “Everyone worked hard and struggled for this justice, for this cause. When they hear it today, everyone will be happy, thank God. I don’t know how to express it or even what to do with myself.”

blocks.caption: The Gambian justice minister Dawda Jallow, centre, speaking at the ICJ in The Hague on Thursday: ‘The victory belongs to the Rohingya. They survived. They testified. And today, they will believe.’ Photograph: Jeroen Jumelet/ANP/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Another Rohingya present, who cannot be named because of safety concerns, said they cried as the judge went through each of the rulings.
